3---  # Typeclasses
4-
5---  Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6---  variable with no constraint on it.
7-
8---  Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
9---      Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
10---      lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
11---
12---      `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
13---
14---      Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?

18-
19---  This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
20---  `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
21---  which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
22---  `a : α`.
23-
24---  Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α`
25---  completely generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,
26---  this is done through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
27---  **typeclasses**. The concept originated in Haskell and is analogous to
28---  features you may know from other languages, such as traits in Rust.
29-
30---  ## Why We Need Typeclasses
31-
32---  Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
33---  occurs in a list:
34-
35-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
36-  match xs with
37-  | [] => false
38-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
39-
40-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
43-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
44-
45-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
46-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
48-
49---  What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
50---  `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a
51---  type variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
52-
53-sf_expect_failure_in
54-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
55-    match xs with
56-    | [] => false
57-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
58-
59---  failed to synthesize instance of type class
60---    BEq α
61-
62---  Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
63-
64---  Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on
65---  a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one
66---  way to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test
67---  to use.
68-
69-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
70-  match xs with
71-  | [] => false
72-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
73-
74-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
75-
76---  This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
77---  supply, the right equality function.
78-
79---  Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the
80---  function explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own.
81---  We specify something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class`
82---  with the needed function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in
83---  Java or a trait in Rust. Particular implementations of that class are
84---  called *instance*; each type can have its own instance of a class. For
85---  functions that would use such instances, we specify the name of the
86---  class in a *instance implicit* on the polymorphic variable that the
87---  instance's function applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class
88---  inside the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate instance
89---  when the function is called.
90-
91---  Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
92-
93-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
94-  match xs with
95-  | [] => false
96-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
97-
98-theorem List.elem_poly_nil {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
99-
100-theorem List.elem_poly_cons {α : Type} [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
101-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
102-
103-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
104-
105---  Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
106---  differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter
107---  `eq`, whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit
108---  `[BEq α]`. The instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq`
109---  must be provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that is
110---  used. Second, whereas `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to
111---  test equality, `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when
112---  we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass.
113---  Finally, whereas `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality
114---  function `Nat.beq` explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in
115---  automatically based on the type `Nat` of the `List`.
116-
117---  Note to developers (xhalo32):
118---      This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes
119---      from `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in
120---      proofs of `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus
121---      `List.elem_poly` and how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
122-
123---  Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the
124---  instance implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was
125---  fully generic — so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for
126---  *every* type `α`, and no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's
127---  search failed.
128-
129---  Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far.
130---  We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how
131---  to define a typeclass in the first place.
132-
133---  ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
134-
135---  `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of
136---  our own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis —
137---  that made `==` resolve automatically above.
138-
139---  Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
140---  defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
141---  `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default
142---  value an explicit parameter:
143-
144-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
145-  match xs with
146-  | [] => defaultValue
147-  | hd :: _ => hd
148-
149-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
150-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
151-
152---  This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an
153---  element of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based
154---  on the type of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
155-
156---  Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things.
157---  One is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the
158---  caller always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some
159---  information about what it should search *for*.
160-
161---  Considering the second problem first: the way to provide this
162---  information is to *name* the data we're after — the **default value**
163---  of a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way
164---  to give this information a name; structures can also bundle together
165---  more than one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we
166---  only need a single field here.
167-
168---  To address the first problem, we need to mark this particular structure
169---  as one Lean should search for automatically — not every
170---  `structure`-typed argument should be.
171-
172---  Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the naming, as a
173---  plain `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`.
174---  Here's the structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can
175---  reuse the name `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
176-
177-namespace DefaultValueScratch
178-
179-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
180-  value : α
181-
182---  A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to
183---  serve as the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is,
184---  by supplying a `Nat` for the `value` field:
185-
186-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
187-  value := 0
188-
189-end DefaultValueScratch
190-
191---  Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the
192---  sort of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs
193---  to for `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by
194---  writing `class` in place of `structure`:
195-
196-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
197-  value : α
198-
199---  We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of
200---  `def`, we use `instance`:
201-
202-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
203-  value := 0
204-
205---  Lean can now find this instance on its own, via *typeclass synthesis*
206---  (or *typeclass inference*) — the same process that found `BEq Nat`
207---  earlier. That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we
208---  rewrote `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the
209---  explicit `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
210-
211-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
212-  match xs with
213-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
214-  | hd :: _ => hd
215-
216-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
217-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
218-
219-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
220-
221---  Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance
222---  named. Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the
223---  `Nat` `0`, Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for
224---  `DefaultValue Nat`. We know this because we are able to prove that
225---  `DefaultValue.value` is equal to `0`.
226-
227---  Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
228---  `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
229-
230-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
231-  value := -1
232-
233---  We can also create instances for polymorphic types, like `Option α`,
234---  whose default is `none`, by giving the instance declaration a
235---  parameter:
236-
237-instance instDefaultValueOption {α : Type} : DefaultValue (Option α) where
238-  value := none
239-
240---  Now, Lean can infer instances for all these types, including inside
241---  `List.headOr`:
242-
243-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
244-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
245-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option Bool) := by rfl
246-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option (List Nat)) := by rfl
247-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := by rfl
248-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := by rfl
249-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
250-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
251-
252---  Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
253-
254-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
255-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
256-example : instDefaultValueOption.value = (none : Option Nat) := by rfl
257-
258---  The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
259-
260-set_option pp.all true in
261-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
262-
263---  @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
264-
265-set_option pp.all true in
266-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
267-
268---  @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
269-
270---  This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
271---  instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search
272---  directly:
273-
274-#synth DefaultValue Nat
275-
276---  instDefaultValueNat
277-
278---  For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as
279---  the `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we
280---  expect at most one instance per type, so this search has a unique
281---  answer.
282-
283---  We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library equivalent, `Inhabited`, to
284---  work later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default
285---  value for a generic type. First, though, let's go back to
286---  `List.elem_poly` and see how its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets
287---  resolved.

289---  ## Using Typeclasses
290-
291---  Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
292---  turned off:
293-
294-set_option pp.notation false in
295-#check 1 == 2
296-
297---  BEq.beq 1 2 : Bool
298-
299---  Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a
300---  field of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
301-
302-sf_recall
303-  class BEq (α : Type) where
304-      beq : α → α → Bool
305-
306---  Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
307---  type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue`
308---  instance above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
309-
310-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
311-  beq := Nat.beq
312-
313---  This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly`
314---  is called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
315---  `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was
316---  equated with `(1 : Nat)`.
317-
318---  ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
319-
320---  Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when
321---  specialized to natural numbers.
322-
323-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
324-  (
325-  induction xs with
326-  | nil =>
327-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_nil, List.elem_nat_nil]
328-    rfl
329-  | cons hd tl ih =>
330-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_cons, List.elem_nat_cons, ih]
331-    rfl)

333---  ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
334-
335---  The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may
336---  carry — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing
337---  constraints on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify
338---  that a type has not just a single element, but two. Here is a first
339---  attempt:
340-
341-sf_experiment
342-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
343-    one : α
344-    two : α
345-
346---  Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one`
347---  and `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses
348---  can carry proofs along with data, so we can write the following to
349---  enforce that `one` and `two` are distinct.
350-
351-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
352-  one : α
353-  two : α
354-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
355-
356---  Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that
357---  now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
358-
359-instance : HasTwo Nat where
360-  one := 1
361-  two := 2
362-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
363-
364---  In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not
365---  possible to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls
366---  to the author to check, informally, that any required invariants are
367---  satisfied, which can lead to bugs.
368-
369---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
370---      HasThree needs either grading attributes or manual grading
371-
372---  ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
373-
374---  Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
375---  `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements,
376---  and give an instance of it for `Nat`.
377-
378-class HasThree (α : Type) where
379-  one : α
380-  two : α
381-  three : α
382-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
383-  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
384-  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
385-
386-instance : HasThree Nat where
387-  one := 1
388-  two := 2
389-  three := 3
390-  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
391-  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
392-  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)

394-namespace Algebra
395-
396---  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to
397---  define mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about
398---  how those operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a
399---  typeclass to define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
400---  includes four things:
401-
402---  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
403-
404---  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
405---    elements of type `α` into one,
406-
407---  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
408---    element", and
409-
410---  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
411-
412---    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
413-
414---    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
415---      associative)
416-
417---  We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
418-
419--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
420-class OpSet (α : Type) where
421-  op : α → α → α
422-
423-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
424-
425-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
426-  id : α
427-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
428-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
429-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
430-
431---  The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
432---  `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
433---  notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of
434---  `OpSet`, similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
435-
436---  As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where
437---  `0` is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s
438---  `OpSet` instance separately, we can define a single instance that
439---  implements both classes.
440-
441-instance : Monoid Nat where
442-  op := Nat.add
443-  id := 0
444-  left_id := by lia
445-  right_id := by lia
446-  assoc := by lia
447-
448---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
449---      Need to come up with a way to grade the data-carrying instances.
450---      What makes this more complicated is that the `op` is fixed but the
451---      `id` is not.
452-
453---  ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
454-
455---  However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid. What is its
456---  identity element?
457-
458-instance : Monoid Nat where
459-  op := Nat.mul
460-  id := (1)
461-  left_id := (by lia)
462-  right_id := (by lia)
463-  assoc := (by lia)
464-
465---  ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
466-
467---  There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
468---  science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as
469---  the operator in question:
470-
471-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
472-  op := List.append
473-  id := ([])
474-  left_id := (by simp)
475-  right_id := (by simp)
476-  assoc := (by simp)
477-
478---  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
479---  properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on
480---  the typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
481---  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the
482---  same set with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
483---  the same:
484-
485-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
486-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
487-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
488-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
489-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
490-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
491-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
492-    rw [h]
493-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
494-    rw [right_id₂]
495-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
496-  exact h'
497-
498---  In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and
499---  `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do
500---  so however, because these are class instances instead of normal
501---  structures, we preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping
502---  through the above proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember
503---  that you can set `set_option pp.all true` or
504---  `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you more clearly what
505---  is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
506---  `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
507---  arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal
508---  as `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
509-
510---  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation
511---  `inv`, which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`.
512---  We can extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
513-
514-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
515-  inv : α → α
516-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
517-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
518-
519---  Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there is no
520---  inverse operation on the natural numbers such that
521---  `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does
522---  form a group over the integers:
523-
524---  ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
525-
526-instance : Group Int where
527-  op := Int.add
528-  id := (0)
529-  inv := (Int.neg)
530-  left_id := (by lia)
531-  right_id := (by lia)
532-  assoc := (by lia)
533-  left_inv := (by lia)
534-  right_inv := (by lia)
535-
536---  The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a rich area of
537---  mathematics. Here, we will only prove a handful of its simplest
538---  results:
539-
540---  Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
541---      This also prints weird.
542-
543---  ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
544-
545---  Two groups defined with the same operation over the same set must have
546---  the same inverse as well.
547-
548-theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
549-  ext a
550-  rw [←g₁.right_id (Group.inv a), ←g₁.right_inv a]
551-  rw [g₁.assoc, h, g₂.left_inv a, g₂.left_id]
552-
553---  Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
554---      Taking suggestions for additional simple group theory theorems to
555---      prove here.
556-
557-end Algebra

559---  ## Maps
560-
561---  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in
562---  ordinary programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're
563---  going to need them in many places in later volumes.
564-
565---  We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a
566---  "default" element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't
567---  exist, and *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate
568---  success or failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps,
569---  using `none` as the default element.
570-
571---  ### Key and Value Types
572-
573---  To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to
574---  index into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. In this
575---  section, we'll use the type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β`
576---  for values. In addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key
577---  type `α` requires instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`
578---  typeclasses:
579-
580-sf_recall
581-  class ReflBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop where
582-      rfl {a : α} : a == a
583-
584-sf_recall
585-  class LawfulBEq (α : Type) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
586-      eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
587-
588---  These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
589---  coincides with proposition equality `=`.
590-
591---  In general, we place no constraints on the value type `β`.
592-
593---  ### Total Maps
594-
595---  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`,
596---  with a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs.
597---  Here, we are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead.
598---  The advantage of this representation is that it offers a more
599---  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic
600---  chapter: two maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
601---  represented as exactly the same function, rather than just as
602---  "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.
603-
604---  Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
605---  `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
606---  contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type
607---  `β`.
608-
609-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
610-  inner : α → β
611-
612-namespace TotalMap
613-
614---  In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
615---  typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
616---  `DefaultValue` example from above:
617-
618---  The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a
619---  default element; this map always returns the default element when
620---  applied to any key.
621-
622-def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
623-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
624-
625---  These types and implicit instances are now available automatically to
626---  all the definitions in this section.
627-
628---  Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
629---  `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
630---  standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with
631---  this empty map.
632-
633-instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
634-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
635-
636-theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
637-
638---  Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat`
639---  values:
640-
641-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
642-
643---  #### Getting Elements
644-
645---  While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood,
646---  we would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface.
647---  Accordingly, we define new operations for querying and updating
648---  mappings. We define a function `get` for getting the value associated
649---  with a key playing the role that `find` played for the Lists chapter's
650---  list-based maps,
651-
652-def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
653-
654-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
655-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
656-theorem get_def {α β : Type} {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
657-
658-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
659-
660---  Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
661-
662-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
663-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
664-  rfl
665-
666---  In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual
667---  `rw` to highlight something interesting. After the rewrites in this
668---  proof, we end up with a goal that looks like
669---  `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`, which we can solve with `rfl`.
670---  This is because the projection `.inner` on a structure of the form
671---  `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
672-
673---  `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
674---  implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because `get_def` "peeks"
675---  through the abstraction, it should be used sparingly, and only inside
676---  the `TotalMap` namespace.
677-
678---  To make element-getting more convenient, let's define notation so we
679---  can write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `emptyNatMap.get`. We could
680---  notate `get` directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but
681---  here we'll instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass,
682---  `MyGetElem`, and notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to
683---  `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not
684---  just `TotalMap`.
685-
686---  Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
687---  notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
688---  already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved
689---  by instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
690---  overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation
691---  for `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a
692---  simpler version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which
693---  has many instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it
694---  to illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
695-
696---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
697---      A reason I can come up with why we use a notation typeclass (in
698---      library code) over a plain notation is that it makes it possible
699---      (for a downstream consumer) to write `open scoped MyGetElem`
700---      instead of writing `open scoped TotalMap` and
701---      `open scoped PartialMap` individually. This wouldn't be a good sell
702---      if `→ₜ` and `→ₚ` are scoped notations, but they're currently
703---      global.
704-
705-end TotalMap
706-
707---  The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
708---  implementation, its keys, and its values.
709-
710-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
711-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
712-
713---  (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
714---  helps typeclass inference.)
715-
716---  The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:
717-
718-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
719-  getElem m a := m.get a
720-
721---  Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
722---  defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter
723---  Lists, including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation
724---  lists back out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with
725---  `infixl`/`infixr` or `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach
726---  for the more general `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the
727---  `m[a]` syntax to work.
728-
729---  Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules`
730---  and the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities. However, if
731---  you do wish to learn more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
732---  4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
733---  contain more detail.
734-
735-namespace MyGetElem
736-
737-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
738-
739-@[app_unexpander getElem]
740-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
741-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
742-  | _ => throw ()
743-end MyGetElem
744-
745-open scoped MyGetElem
746-
747---  Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]` syntax for
748---  `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation`
749---  as we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override
750---  the default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem`
751---  is in force.
752-
753---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
754---      Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...
755-
756---  Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use
757---  the notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.
758-
759-namespace TotalMap
760-
761-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
762-
763-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
764-
765-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
766-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
767-
768---  We want the public API of `TotalMap` to use the `m[a]` notation instead
769---  of `m.get a` so we provide the reverse direction of `getElem_def` as a
770---  `simp` lemma; the `m[a]` notation is the `TotalMap` API's `simp` normal
771---  form.
772-
773-@[simp]
774-theorem get_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := rfl
775-
776-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
777-  simp
778-
779---  This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def` outside concrete
780---  examples (which are typically solvable with `rfl` anyways).
781-
782---  #### Updating Elements
783-
784---  Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`,
785---  and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes
786---  every other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map
787---  function around the old one.
788-
789-def update {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) [BEq α] (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
790-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
791-
792---  For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where
793---  `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped
794---  to `false`, like this:
795-
796-def exampleMap :=
797-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
798-    |>.update "foo" true
799-    |>.update "bar" true
800-
801---  Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`,
802---  letting us chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right
803---  without nested parentheses.
804-
805---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
806---      Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there good places
807---      to use it earlier?)
808-
809---  We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
810---  going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules`
811---  machinery as we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that
812---  references `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update`
813---  doesn't need to work generically across container types (there's no
814---  standard-library operation like `GetElem` that we're mirroring here),
815---  so the simpler, direct route suffices.
816-
817-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
818-
819-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
820-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
821-theorem update_def {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
822-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
823-
824-theorem update_apply {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
825-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl
826-
827---  We can omit the map from the notation when we want it to be empty:
828-
829-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
830-
831---  The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
832-
833-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
834-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
835-
836-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := by rfl
837-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := by rfl
838-
839-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by rfl
840-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by rfl
841-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by rfl
842-
843---  Let's also see a couple of examples of working with updated maps using
844---  rewrites:
845-
846-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by
847-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
848-
849-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by
850-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "foo") = false by simp, cond_false]
851-  rw [update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
852-
853-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by
854-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "quux") = false by simp, cond_false]
855-  rw [update_apply, show ("foo" == "quux") = false by rfl, cond_false]
856-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def, Bool.default_bool]
857-
858---  When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several fundamental facts
859---  about how they behave.
860-
861---  Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure you
862---  thoroughly understand the statements of the lemmas!
863-
864---  (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality axiom
865---  `funext`, discussed in the Logic chapter.)
866-
867---  First, the empty map returns its default element for all keys:
868-
869-@[simp]
870-theorem getElem_empty {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := by
871-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def]
872-
873---  Notice that in the example `exampleMap'["quux"] = false` the last
874---  rewrite is effectively just `getElem_empty`.
875-
876---  Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value `b` and then
877---  look up `a` in the map resulting from the `update`, we get back `b`:
878-
879-@[simp]
880-theorem update_eq {α β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
881-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, get_def]
882-  dsimp only -- reduces `{ inner := ... }.inner` so that we get a subterm that looks like `a == a`
883-  rw [BEq.rfl, cond_true]
884-
885---  On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and then look
886---  up a *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we get the same result
887---  that `m` would have given:
888-
889---  ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq (Optional) ⭐⭐
890-
891-@[simp]
892-theorem update_neq {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
893-    (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
894-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, get_def]
895-  dsimp only
896-  rw [beq_false_of_ne h, cond_false]
897-
898---  The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we first need
899---  to say when two maps are equal. Since a total map is implemented as a
900---  function, this is effectively the functional extensionality principle
901---  (`funext`) from the Logic chapter: two maps are equal when they agree
902---  at every key. Recording it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets
903---  the `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the
904---  proofs below.
905-
906---  The fact that `TotalMap` is a structure complicates things slightly. We
907---  need to use injectivity of its constructor `mk` which Lean
908---  automatically provides for us as `mk.injEq`. It lets us prove `m₁ = m₂`
909---  from `m₁.inner = m₂.inner` or vice versa.
910-
911-@[ext]
912-theorem ext {α β : Type} {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := by
913-  rw [TotalMap.mk.injEq]
914-  apply funext
915-  intro x
916-  specialize h x
917-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, getElem_def, get_def] at h
918-  exact h
919-
920---  To demonstrate this extensionality principle, let's look at an example:
921-
922-example : "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true = "foo" →ₜ true ; "bar" →ₜ true := by
923-  ext a
924-  by_cases h : "bar" = a
925-  · subst h
926-    rw [update_eq, update_neq (show "foo" ≠ "bar" by simp), update_eq]
927-  · simp only [update_apply]
928-    rw [beq_false_of_ne h]
929-    simp
930-
931---  Given keys `a₁` and `a₂`, the tactic `by_cases` `h : a₁ = a₂` splits
932---  the proof into the case where they are equal — where `subst h` then
933---  replaces one by the other — and the case where they are not, which is
934---  what `update_neq` wants. Use it to prove the following theorem, which
935---  states that if we update a map to assign key `a` the same value as it
936---  already has in `m`, then the result is equal to `m`:
937-
938---  ### Exercise (2 stars): update_same ⭐⭐
939-
940-@[simp]
941-theorem update_same {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : (a →ₜ m[a] ; m) = m := by
942-  ext a'
943-  by_cases h : a = a'
944-  · subst h
945-    simp
946-  · simp [update_neq h]
947-
948---  Similarly, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and
949---  then update again with the same key `a` and another value `b₂`, the
950---  resulting map behaves the same (gives the same result when applied to
951---  any key) as the simpler map obtained by performing just the second
952---  `update` on `m`:
953-
954---  ### Exercise (2 stars): update_shadow (Optional) ⭐⭐
955-
956-@[simp]
957-theorem update_shadow {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
958-    (a →ₜ b₂ ; a →ₜ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₜ b₂ ; m) := by
959-  ext a'
960-  by_cases h : a = a'
961-  · subst h
962-    simp
963-  · simp [update_neq h]
964-

1027---  ### Exercise (3 stars): update_permute ⭐⭐⭐
1028-
1029-theorem update_permute {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
1030-    (a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; m) := by
1031-  ext a'

1037-    · subst h₂

1049---  ### Notation for Concrete Maps
1050-

1321---  In this section, we will make use of some definitions and theorems
1322---  about natural numbers that we discussed and proved in previous
1323---  chapters; copy your solutions to those problems here:
1324-
1325-namespace Nat
1326-
1327-def even (n : Nat) :=
1328-  match n with
1329-  | 0     => true
1330-  | 1     => false
1331-  | n + 2 => even n

1334-

1336-    even (n + 1) = !(even n) := by
1337-  induction n with
1338-  | zero =>
1339-    rfl
1340-  | succ n' ih =>
1341-    rw [even, ih, Bool.not_not]

1349-

1356---  We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean:
1357---  with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1358-
1359---  Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1360-
1361---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1362---      Check formatting:
1363-
1364---  - ⠀
1365---  - `Bool`
1366---  - `Prop`
1367---  - decidable?
1368---  - yes
1369---  - no
1370---  - useable with `match`?
1371---  - yes
1372---  - no
1373---  - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1374---  - no
1375---  - yes
1376-
1377---  The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1378---  (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1379---  number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a
1380---  terminating mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
1381---  true.
1382-
1383---  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only
1384---  by functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false`
1385---  in finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1386---  argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether
1387---  a given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1388-
1389---  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1390---  mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1391---  contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1392---  halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this
1393---  essential difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a
1394---  boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or
1395---  `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1396-
1397---  The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1398---  functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly
1399---  to justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1400---  required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1401---  properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property
1402---  that happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean
1403---  computation or as a function into Prop.
1404-
1405---  As an example, we can write

1408-
1409---  or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.

1411-example : Nat.Even 42 := by exists 21

1413---  Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1414---  evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1415-

1418-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
1419-  induction k with
1420-  | zero =>
1421-    rewrite [Nat.double_zero, Nat.even_zero]
1422-    rfl
1423-  | succ n ih =>
1424-    rewrite [Nat.double_succ, Nat.even_succ, Nat.even_succ, Bool.not_not]
1425-    exact ih

1429-theorem even_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1430-    ∃ (k : Nat), n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by (
1431-  induction n with
1432-  | zero =>
1433-    exists 0
1434-  | succ n ih =>
1435-    obtain ⟨k, ih⟩ := ih

1437-    by_cases h : Nat.even n
1438-    · exists k
1439-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1440-      subst ih

1442-    · exists k + 1
1443-      rewrite [Bool.not_eq_true] at h
1444-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1445-      subst ih
1446-      rewrite [cond_false, Bool.not_false, cond_true]
1447-      rfl)

1557---  `if` statement, we are allowed to write

1559-def nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1560-
1561---  Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of natural
1562---  numbers is decidable, and Lean makes use of this fact. If we print this
1563---  definition with notation unset, we would find that it is using
1564---  `instDecidableEqNat`
1565-
1566-set_option pp.all true in
1567-#print nat_eq
1568-
1569---  which proves that this equality is decidable.
1570-
1571---  This is only half the story however: while Lean's core theory enables
1572---  this computation, Lean is also often used in applications where we
1573---  don't care about computability, such as pure mathematics. In
1574---  particular, it is possible to write a function for arbitrary equality:
1575-
1576-sf_experiment
1577-  open scoped Classical in
1578-  noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1579-  
1580-  set_option pp.all true in
1581-  #print eq
1582-
1583---  But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and
1584---  `Classical` namespace, that we are *not* interested in computation.
1585---  What is happening in the background is that this allows typeclass
1586---  synthesis to find the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which
1587---  makes use of the axiom of choice to provide a proof that all
1588---  propositions are *classically* decidable. This sort of definition is
1589---  suitable for use with proofs, but is not allowed to be used in
1590---  conjunction with computational features of Lean such as the `decide`
1591---  tactic or the `#eval` command.
1592-
1593---  ## TODO

1600---      carries the proposition and not the boolean, so one direction of

SFLCompat/Experiment.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Experiment
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure_in`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure_in` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure_in
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure_in"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure_in` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure_in?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-
187-namespace Tests
188-
189-/--
190-@ +3:11...+4:8
191-info: unexpected token '#check'; expected 'with'
192----

SFLCompat/Recall/Check.lean

1-module
2-
3--- For testing cases in this file
4-meta import all Init.Prelude
5-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
6-
7-/-!
8-# Recall, checked by elaboration
9-
10-`sf_recall` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
11-development while the build checks that the restatement means the same
12-thing. The restated declaration is elaborated for real, inside a hidden
13-namespace, and compared with the original up to definitional equality; the
14-temporary declaration is then rolled back.
15-
16-Two forms:
17-
18-```
19-sf_recall
20-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
21-
22-sf_recall statement twice_id : twice id 3 = 3
23-```
24-
25-What is compared:
26-
27-* types, always;
28-* a `def`'s value, safety, and abbreviation status;
29-* an inductive's constructors, one by one (names, parameter and index
30-  counts, and each constructor's type);
31-* a structure's fields, field defaults, and type-class registration;
32-* a theorem's statement, never its proof.
33-
34-So a recalled definition may be reformatted or rephrased into something
35-definitionally equal, and a theorem may be reproved differently or, with
36-the `statement` form, restated without any proof. The command is global and
37-available wherever this module is imported.
38--/
39-
40-
41-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Check
42-
43-open Lean Elab Command Meta
44-
45-meta section
46-
47-structure DeclId where
48-  /-- This could be a private name. -/
49-  actual : Name
50-  display : Name
51-
52-def DeclId.ofActual (actual : Name) : DeclId :=
53-  { actual, display := privateToUserName actual }
54-
55-/-- Look up the actual name in temp elaboration namespace -/
56-def tempDeclId (userName : Name) : CommandElabM DeclId := do
57-  let env ← getEnv
58-  let privateName := mkPrivateName env userName
59-  let actual ←
60-    if env.contains privateName then pure privateName
61-    else if env.contains userName then pure userName
62-    else throwError "the re-elaborated declaration '{userName}' was not found"
63-  return .ofActual actual
64-
65-def renameBackName (chk orig n : Name) : Name :=
66-  if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig
67-  else
68-    let chk := privateToUserName chk
69-    if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig else n
70-
71-/--
72-Replaces the name prefix `chk` with `orig` in every constant that `e`
73-mentions: `chk` itself becomes `orig`, and a longer name such as a hidden
74-constructor `chk.mk` becomes `orig.mk`. Constructor types mention the
75-hidden inductive type's name in argument and resulting positions, so this
76-rewrite is what makes a re-elaborated declaration comparable with the
77-original.
78--/
79-def renameBack (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
80-  e.replace fun
81-    | .const n us =>
82-      let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
83-      if n == n' then none else some (.const n' us)
84-    | _ => none
85-
86-/--
87-Applies `renameBack` to the expressions recorded in an info tree. The info
88-recorded while elaborating the hidden copy mentions the hidden constants,
89-so hovers over a recalled declaration would otherwise display the hidden
90-names; rewriting before the trees are stored makes them display the
91-originals, which also exist after the hidden copy is rolled back.
92--/
93-partial def renameBackInfoTree (chk orig : DeclId) (t : InfoTree) : InfoTree :=
94-  match t with
95-  | .context (.parentDeclCtx n) t' =>
96-    .context (.parentDeclCtx (renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n))
97-      (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
98-  | .context ctx t' => .context ctx (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
99-  | .node i children =>
100-    let i := match i with
101-      | .ofTermInfo ti => .ofTermInfo (reTerm ti)
102-      | .ofDelabTermInfo dti => .ofDelabTermInfo { dti with toTermInfo := reTerm dti.toTermInfo }
103-      | other => other
104-    .node i (children.map (renameBackInfoTree chk orig))
105-  | .hole m => .hole m
106-where
107-  reTerm (ti : TermInfo) : TermInfo :=
108-    { ti with
109-      expr := renameBack chk orig ti.expr
110-      expectedType? := ti.expectedType?.map (renameBack chk orig) }
111-
112-/-- A specialization of universe parameters to a declaration.
113-  It stores level parameters of a `ConstantInfo` and mvars created from these parameters.
114--/
115-abbrev Specialization := List Name × List Level
116-
117-def renameBackS (specialization? : Option Specialization)
118-    (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
119-  match specialization? with
120-  | none => renameBack chk orig e
121-  | some (_params, levels) =>
122-    e.replace fun
123-      | .const n _ =>
124-        let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
125-        if n == n' then none else some <| .const n' levels
126-      | _ => none
127-
128-def levelsFor (specialization : Specialization) (info : ConstantInfo) :
129-    TermElabM (List Level) :=
130-  let (params, levels) := specialization
131-  info.levelParams.mapM fun param =>
132-    match params.findIdx? (· == param) with
133-    | some index => pure levels[index]!
134-    | none => throwError
135-      "universe parameter '{param}' of '{info.name}' is not a parameter of the recalled declaration"
136-
137-/--
138-Checks that the types of the original constant `x` and its re-elaborated
139-counterpart `chk` agree, definitionally. The restated type is first
140-rewritten by `renameBack renChk renOrig`; the defaults compare a
141-declaration against its own hidden copy, and the constructor check
142-overrides them with the enclosing inductive types, whose names the
143-constructor types mention. The restatement's universe parameters are
144-instantiated with the original's.
145--/
146-def checkTypesMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
147-    (specialization? : Option Specialization)
148-    (renChk : DeclId := chk) (renOrig : DeclId := x) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
149-    TermElabM Unit := do
150-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
151-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
152-  if specialization?.isNone then
153-    -- no specialization, do strict check first
154-    unless origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length do
155-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
156-  let origType ← match specialization? with
157-    | none => pure origInfo.type
158-    | some s => origInfo.instantiateTypeLevelParams <$> levelsFor s origInfo
159-  let chkType := match specialization? with
160-    | none => (renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type).instantiateLevelParams
161-        chkInfo.levelParams (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
162-    | some _ => renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type
163-  unless ← isDefEq chkType origType do
164-    throwErrorAt ref
165-      (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
166-          Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD chkType}" ++ hint)
167-
168-/--
169-All constructor syntax nodes of a command, in source order: an inductive
170-type's `| name : ...` alternatives and a structure's `name ::` header.
171--/
172-partial def ctorStxs (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
173-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap ctorStxs
174-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor
175-      || stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
176-    #[stx] ++ inner
177-  else inner
178-
179-/-- Does the syntax contain a doc comment? -/
180-def hasDocComment (stx : Syntax) : Bool :=
181-  (stx.find? (·.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.docComment)).isSome
182-
183-/--
184-Suggestions localized to a mismatched constructor, returned as a pair of
185-hints for name errors and for type errors. An inductive type's `| name : ...` alternative is replaced
186-with the original constructor's own source. A structure's `name ::` header
187-can carry a name fix but not a field fix, so its type errors keep `outer`,
188-the suggestion that replaces the whole restatement. A constructor without
189-syntax also falls back to `outer`.
190--/
191-def ctorHints (ctorRef : Syntax) (origCtor origShort : Name) (outer : MessageData) :
192-    TermElabM (MessageData × MessageData) := do
193-  try
194-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor then
195-      let origSrc := dedent (← sourceOf origCtor)
196-      -- A restatement without a doc comment gets a suggestion without one;
197-      -- the meaning check does not compare documentation.
198-      let origSrc := if hasDocComment ctorRef then origSrc
199-        else stripLeadingComments origSrc
200-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
201-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef origSrc restatedSrc
202-      return (h, h)
203-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
204-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
205-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef s!"{origShort} ::" restatedSrc
206-      return (h, outer)
207-    return (outer, outer)
208-  catch _ => return (outer, outer)
209-
210-/--
211-Checks a re-elaborated declaration against the original, definitionally.
212-Errors point at `ref`, the restated command, except for constructor
213-mismatches, which point at the offending constructor within it.
214--/
215-def checkMatchCore (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
216-    (specialization? : Option (List Name × List Level))
217-    (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
218-  checkTypesMatch x chk ref specialization? (hint := hint)
219-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
220-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
221-  match origInfo, chkInfo with
222-  | .defnInfo orig, .defnInfo restated =>
223-    let origVal ← match specialization? with
224-      | none => pure orig.value
225-      | some s => origInfo.instantiateValueLevelParams! <$> levelsFor s origInfo
226-    let chkVal := match specialization? with
227-      | none => (renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value).instantiateLevelParams
228-          restated.levelParams (orig.levelParams.map .param)
229-      | some _ => renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value
230-    unless ← isDefEq chkVal origVal do
231-      throwErrorAt ref
232-        (m!"the value of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
233-            Original:{indentD orig.value}\nRestated:{indentD chkVal}" ++ hint)
234-  | .inductInfo orig, .inductInfo restated =>
235-    unless orig.numParams == restated.numParams && orig.numIndices == restated.numIndices do
236-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"parameters or indices of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
237-    unless orig.ctors.length == restated.ctors.length do
238-      throwErrorAt ref
239-        (m!"'{x.display}' has {orig.ctors.length} constructors, \
240-            the restatement has {restated.ctors.length}" ++ hint)
241-    -- A `structure` that writes no `name ::` header has a constructor
242-    -- without syntax; the whole command remains the fallback position.
243-    let ctorRefs := ctorStxs ref
244-    let mut i := 0
245-    for origCtorActual in orig.ctors, chkCtorActual in restated.ctors do
246-      let origCtor := DeclId.ofActual origCtorActual
247-      let chkCtor := DeclId.ofActual chkCtorActual
248-      let ctorRef := ctorRefs[i]?.getD ref
249-      let origShort := origCtor.actual.replacePrefix x.actual .anonymous
250-      let (nameHint, typeHint) ← ctorHints ctorRef origCtor.actual origShort hint
251-      let renamedChkCtor := DeclId.ofActual <|
252-        chkCtor.actual.replacePrefix chk.actual x.actual
253-      unless origCtor.actual == renamedChkCtor.actual do
254-        throwErrorAt ctorRef
255-          (m!"constructor '{renamedChkCtor.display}' does not match \
256-              '{origCtor.display}'" ++ nameHint)
257-      checkTypesMatch origCtor chkCtor ctorRef specialization?
258-        (renChk := chk) (renOrig := x) (hint := typeHint)
259-      i := i + 1
260-    -- A structure's field names are part of its interface, and the
261-    -- constructor's type does not record them, so they are compared
262-    -- through the environment's structure information.
263-    let env ← getEnv
264-    match getStructureInfo? env x.actual, getStructureInfo? env chk.actual with
265-    | some origSi, some chkSi =>
266-      let origFields := origSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
267-      let chkFields := chkSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
268-      unless origFields.map (·.actual) == chkFields.map (·.actual) do
269-        throwErrorAt ref
270-          (m!"the fields of '{x.display}' do not match.\n\
271-              Original:{indentD (toMessageData (origFields.map (·.display)).toList)}\n\
272-              Restated:{indentD (toMessageData (chkFields.map (·.display)).toList)}" ++ hint)
273-      unless getOutParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutParamPositions? env chk.actual
274-          && getOutLevelParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutLevelParamPositions? env chk.actual do
275-        throwErrorAt ref (m!"the type-class metadata of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
276-    | some _, none =>
277-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is a structure, but the restatement is not" ++ hint)
278-    | none, some _ =>
279-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is not a structure, but the restatement is one" ++ hint)
280-    | none, none => pure ()
281-  -- A theorem's proof is not compared; restating it as a `def` is also
282-  -- accepted, since only the statement matters.
283-  | .thmInfo _, .thmInfo _ => pure ()
284-  | .thmInfo _, .defnInfo _ => pure ()
285-  | .axiomInfo _, .axiomInfo _ => pure ()
286-  | .opaqueInfo _, .opaqueInfo _ => pure ()
287-  | _, _ =>
288-    throwErrorAt ref
289-      (m!"'{x.display}' and its restatement are different kinds of declaration" ++ hint)

291-/--
292-Run `checkpointDefEq` in `TermElabM`.
293-Note: this is only for universe level constraints solving in `isDefEq` and
294-has nothing to do with the elaborator.
295--/
296-def checkpointDefEq' (action : TermElabM Bool) : TermElabM Bool :=
297-  controlAt MetaM fun runInBase =>
298-    checkpointDefEq (mayPostpone := false) (runInBase action)
299-
300-def checkMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
301-    (strictUniverse : Bool) (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
302-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
303-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
304-  if origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length then
305-    -- if the definition being to check has exactly the same number of the parameters,
306-    -- treat it as no specialization in checking
307-    checkMatchCore x chk ref none hint
308-  else if !strictUniverse && !origInfo.levelParams.isEmpty && chkInfo.levelParams.isEmpty then
309-    -- if all parameters have been specified (monomorphic), do check with specialization
310-    let succeeded ← checkpointDefEq' do
311-      let levels ← mkFreshLevelMVarsFor origInfo
312-      checkMatchCore x chk ref (some (origInfo.levelParams, levels)) hint
313-      pure true
314-    unless succeeded do
315-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
316-  else
317-    throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
318-
319-
320-/--
321-`sf_recall` restates a definition from earlier in the development and checks
322-that the restatement means the same thing. `sf_recall statement x : T` checks
323-that `T` matches the statement of the theorem `x`.
324--/
325-syntax (name := recallChk) "sf_recall " command : command
326-
327-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
328-syntax (name := recallChkStrict) "sf_recall" " +" noWs &"strictUniverse" ppSpace command : command
329-
330-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
331-syntax (name := recallChkStmt) "sf_recall " &"statement " ident " : " term : command
332-
333-
334-def elabRecallCommand (cmd : Syntax) (strictUniverse : Bool) : CommandElabM Unit := do
335-  let decl ← declaredName cmd
336-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
337-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
338-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
339-  -- The restatement elaborates unchanged inside a fresh hidden namespace:
340-  -- self-references (an inductive's own name in its constructor types, in
341-  -- resulting-type position included) resolve to the hidden copy, and
342-  -- every other name resolves as it would at the recall site. The
343-  -- namespace comes from the name generator: `_uniq` names cannot be
344-  -- written in source, so it is collision-free, and unlike a macro-scoped
345-  -- name it is an ordinary component, so declarations under it keep the
346-  -- prefix structure that `renameBack` and the constructor comparison
347-  -- rely on.
348-  let ns ← liftCoreM (mkFreshId : CoreM Name)
349-  -- Any mismatch gets a clickable fix: replace the restatement with the
350-  -- original's source text, indented like the restatement. The helpers
351-  -- for recovering and re-indenting source are shared with the
352-  -- byte-for-byte variant.
353-  -- A failed hint must not fail the check: not every constant has a
354-  -- declaration range or sources on the search path.
355-  let hint ←
356-    try
357-      let original := dedent (← sourceOf x.actual)
358-      let original := if hasDocComment cmd then original
359-        else stripLeadingComments original
360-      let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
361-      liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd original restated
362-    catch _ => pure .nil
363-  let envBefore ← getEnv
364-  try
365-    let chk ← withScope (fun sc => { sc with currNamespace := sc.currNamespace ++ ns }) do
366-      let saved ← getResetInfoTrees
367-      try
368-        elabCommand cmd
369-        -- this could be a private name
370-        let userName := (← getScope).currNamespace ++ decl.written
371-        let chk ← tempDeclId userName
372-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
373-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner.map (renameBackInfoTree chk x) }
374-        return chk
375-      catch e =>
376-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
377-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner }
378-        throw e
379-    runTermElabM fun _ => checkMatch x chk cmd strictUniverse (hint := hint)
380-  finally
381-    setEnv envBefore
382-
383-def elabRecallStatement (ident stmt : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
384-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
385-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo ident
386-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
387-  addConstInfo ident x.actual
388-  let region := mkNullNode #[ident, stmt]
389-  let restated ← sourceOfSyntax region
390-  runTermElabM fun _ => do
391-    -- The suggestion restates the original's type as the pretty-printer
392-    -- renders it. The statement cannot be carved out of the original's
393-    -- source, since finding its boundary would require parsing the
394-    -- source in the elaboration context of its declaration site.
395-    let hint ←
396-      try
397-        let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
398-        let printed ← ppExpr origInfo.type
399-        replaceWithOriginalHint region
400-          s!"{ident.getId} : {printed}" restated
401-      catch _ => pure .nil
402-    let t ← Term.elabType stmt
403-    Term.synthesizeSyntheticMVarsNoPostponing
404-    let t ← instantiateMVars (← Term.levelMVarToParam t)
405-    let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
406-    let stParams := (collectLevelParams {} t).params
407-    unless stParams.size == origInfo.levelParams.length do
408-      throwErrorAt stmt (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
409-    let t := t.instantiateLevelParams stParams.toList
410-      (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
411-    unless ← isDefEq t origInfo.type do
412-      throwErrorAt stmt
413-        (m!"the restated statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
414-            Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD t}" ++ hint)
415-
416-
417-elab_rules : command
418-  | `(sf_recall $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd false
419-  | `(sf_recall +strictUniverse $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd true
420-  | `(sf_recall statement $ident:ident : $stmt:term) => elabRecallStatement ident stmt
421-
422-end
