11-partial def declIds (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
12-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap declIds
13-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.declId then #[stx] ++ inner else inner
14-
15-/-- The syntax and written name of the single declaration in a recall command. -/
16-structure DeclSyntax where
17-  ident : Syntax
18-  written : Name
19-
20-/--
21-The `declId` node of a declaration command, together with the name written
22-in it. A command that declares several names (a `mutual` block) or none (an
23-anonymous `instance`, an `example`) is rejected.
24--/
25-def declaredName (cmd : Syntax) : CommandElabM DeclSyntax := do
26-  let defined := declIds cmd
27-  match h : defined.size with
28-  | 0 => throwErrorAt cmd "the restated command does not declare a name"
29-  | 1 =>
30-    let declId := defined[0]
31-    return { ident := declId[0], written := declId[0].getId }
32-  | n + 2 =>
33-    for h : i in 0...(n + 1) do
34-      logErrorAt defined[i]
35-        "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
36-    throwErrorAt defined[n + 1]
37-      "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
38-
39-/--
40-Removes the block indentation of a declaration's source text. The first
41-line starts at the declaration's first token and has no indentation of its
42-own; each following line is stripped of the smallest indentation found
43-among the non-blank ones. Restatements of the same text at different block
44-depths dedent to identical strings, and every other difference survives
45-dedenting.
46--/
47-def dedent (s : String) : String :=
48-  match indentWidth s, s.splitOn "\n" with
49-  | some n, first :: rest =>
50-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map (fun l => String.ofList (l.toList.drop n)))
51-  | _, _ => s
52-where
53-  /-- The smallest indentation among the non-blank continuation lines. -/
54-  indentWidth (s : String) : Option Nat :=
55-    s.splitOn "\n" |>.drop 1 |>.map (·.toList)
56-      |>.filter (fun l => !l.all (·.isWhitespace))
57-      |>.map (fun l => (l.takeWhile (· == ' ')).length)
58-      |>.min?
59-
60-/--
61-Indents the continuation lines of dedented source text by `n` spaces, so
62-that the text reads correctly at the block depth of a restatement.
63--/
64-def reindent (s : String) (n : Nat) : String :=
65-  match s.splitOn "\n" with
66-  | [] => s
67-  | first :: rest =>
68-    let pad := String.ofList (List.replicate n ' ')
69-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map fun l =>
70-      if l.toList.all (·.isWhitespace) then l else pad ++ l)
71-
72-/--
73-Removes the comments from the front of dedented source text, together with
74-the whitespace around them, so that a suggestion offered for a restatement
75-that carries no comments does not introduce any. The text of a declaration
76-or of a constructor begins with its doc comment when it has one, possibly
77-accompanied by ordinary comments, and a leading block comment ends at its
78-depth-balanced closing delimiter, so a character scan recognizes the
79-leading run of comments exactly. A comment elsewhere in the text cannot be
80-recognized without lexing and is left in place.
81--/
82-def stripLeadingComments (s : String) : String := Id.run do
83-  let mut cs := s.toList.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
84-  repeat
85-    if cs.take 2 == ['/', '-'] then
86-      cs := cs.drop 2
87-      let mut depth := 1
88-      while depth > 0 do
89-        match cs with
90-        | [] => return s
91-        | '/' :: '-' :: rest => depth := depth + 1; cs := rest
92-        | '-' :: '/' :: rest => depth := depth - 1; cs := rest
93-        | _ :: rest => cs := rest
94-    else if cs.take 2 == ['-', '-'] then
95-      cs := cs.dropWhile (· != '\n')
96-    else
97-      break
98-    cs := cs.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
99-  return String.ofList cs
100-
101-/--
102-A clickable suggestion that replaces the restated text at `span` with
103-`original`, which must already be dedented. The original's indentation is
104-moved to match the restatement's: the restatement's own indentation width
105-when it has continuation lines, one step past the span's start column when
106-it does not.
107--/
108-def replaceWithOriginalHint [Monad m] [MonadFileMap m] [MonadLiftT CoreM m]
109-    (span : Syntax) (original restated : String) : m MessageData := do
110-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
111-  let k := match dedent.indentWidth restated, span.getRange? with
112-    | some k, _ => k
113-    | none, some r => (fileMap.toPosition r.start).column + 2
114-    | none, none => 2
115-  MessageData.hint m!"Replace the restatement with the original:"
116-    #[{ suggestion := .string (reindent original k), span? := some span }]
117-
118-/--
119-The source text of the declaration of `x`, from the file that declared it.
120-
121-The location comes from the declaration range that Lean records for every
122-constant. A declaration from the current file is read out of the file map;
123-one from an imported module is read from its source file, found on the
124-source search path. In a book build the whole project's sources are on that
125-path, so definitions can be recalled across chapters.
126--/
127-def sourceOf [Monad m] [MonadEnv m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
128-    [MonadLiftT IO m] [MonadLiftT BaseIO m] (x : Name) : m String := do
129-  let some ranges ← findDeclarationRanges? x
130-    | throwError "no declaration range recorded for '{x}'"
131-  let env ← getEnv
132-  let text ←
133-    match env.getModuleIdxFor? x with
134-    | none => pure (← getFileMap)
135-    | some idx => do
136-      let modName := env.allImportedModuleNames[idx.toNat]!
137-      let sp ← getSrcSearchPath
138-      let some path ← sp.findModuleWithExt "lean" modName
139-        | throwError "source for module '{modName}' is not on the search path"
140-      pure (FileMap.ofString (← IO.FS.readFile path))
141-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract text.source
142-    (text.ofPosition ranges.range.pos) (text.ofPosition ranges.range.endPos)
143-
144-/-- The source text of a piece of syntax in the current file. -/
145-def sourceOfSyntax [Monad m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
146-    (stx : Syntax) : m String := do
147-  let some r := stx.getRange?
148-    | throwErrorAt stx "no source range"
149-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract (← getFileMap).source r.start r.stop
150-
151-end
152-
153-end SFLCompat.Recall

SFLCompat/Recall/Source.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
4-
5-/-!
6-# Recall, checked byte for byte
7-
8-`sf_recall_source` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
9-development while the build checks that the restatement matches the
10-original's source text, byte for byte. The restated text is what the
11-reader already saw, and it can never drift from the original.
12-
13-```
14-sf_recall_source
15-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
16-```
17-
18-The restated declaration is parsed but never elaborated; the check is
19-purely textual: after the block indentation is removed from each side, the
20-two texts must be equal, byte for byte. The restatement may sit at a
21-different indentation depth, but it may not be reflowed or respaced.
22-
23-The comparison covers whole declarations only. Carving a statement out of
24-the original's source would require parsing it, which is only possible in
25-the elaboration context of its declaration site; restating only a theorem
26-statement is therefore the province of `sf_recall statement`, which compares
27-elaborated types.
28--/
29-
30-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Source
31-
32-open Lean Elab Command
33-
34-/--
35-`recall_source` restates a definition from earlier in the development and
36-checks that the restatement matches the original's source text, byte for
37-byte, modulo block indentation.
38--/
39-syntax (name := recallSrc) "sf_recall_source " command : command
40-
41-elab_rules : command
42-  | `(sf_recall_source $cmd:command) => do
43-    let decl ← declaredName cmd
44-    let x ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
45-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
46-    -- The restatement is never elaborated, so it produces no info of its
47-    -- own. The whole compared region is one big reference to the original:
48-    -- hovering anywhere in it shows the original, and go-to-definition
49-    -- jumps to it.
50-    addConstInfo cmd x
51-    let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
52-    let original ← sourceOf x
53-    unless dedent restated == dedent original do
54-      throwErrorAt cmd
55-        (m!"the restatement of '{privateToUserName x}' does not match its source.\n\
56-            Original:{indentD original}\nRestated:{indentD restated}"
57-          ++ (← liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd (dedent original) restated))
58-
59-namespace Tests
60-
61-inductive Palette where
62-  | red | green | blue
63-
64-def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
65-
66-theorem twice_id : twice id 3 = 3 := rfl
67-
68-sf_recall_source
69-  inductive Palette where
70-    | red | green | blue
71-
72-sf_recall_source
73-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
74-
75--- Leading comments are removed exactly, including the one-line, nested,
76--- and line-comment forms; text without them is untouched.
77-#guard SFLCompat.Recall.stripLeadingComments
78-  "/-- d -/ theorem foo : True := trivial" == "theorem foo : True := trivial"
79-#guard SFLCompat.Recall.stripLeadingComments
80-  "/-- a /- b -/ c -/\ndef x := 1" == "def x := 1"
81-#guard SFLCompat.Recall.stripLeadingComments
82-  "/-- d -/\n-- note\n-- more\ndef x := 1" == "def x := 1"
83-#guard SFLCompat.Recall.stripLeadingComments "def x := 1" == "def x := 1"
84-
85-/--
86-error: the restatement of 'SFLCompat.Recall.Source.Tests.twice' does not match its source.
87-Original:
88-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
89-Restated:
90-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
91-
92-Hint: Replace the restatement with the original:
93-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <̵|̵ ̵(̲f n)̲
94--/
95-#guard_msgs in
96-sf_recall_source
97-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
98-
99--- Reflowing the original is rejected even though the tokens agree.
100-/--
101-error: the restatement of 'SFLCompat.Recall.Source.Tests.twice' does not match its source.
102-Original:
103-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)

106-      f (f n)
107-
108-Hint: Replace the restatement with the original:
109-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
110-  ̵  ̵ ̵ ̵f (f n)
111--/
112-#guard_msgs in
113-sf_recall_source
114-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
115-    f (f n)
116-
117-/--
118-error: the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time
119----
120-error: the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time
121--/
122-#guard_msgs in
123-sf_recall_source

TS/Slang.lean

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---      We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7---      proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8---      width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9-
10---  In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to
11---  use Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin
12---  to shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
13---  programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call
14---  **Slang** (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets
15---  us introduce key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics*
16---  of programming languages and show how those concepts are realized in
17---  Lean.
18-
19---  (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
20---  Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked
21---  through it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next
22---  chapter of this one.)
23-
24---  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
25-
26---  Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
27---  sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
28-
29---  ### Syntax
30-
31-namespace Slang
32-
33---  These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
34---  boolean expressions.
35-
36-inductive Aexp where
37-  | num (n : Nat)
38-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
39-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
40-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
41-
42-inductive Bexp where
43-  | bool (b : Bool)
44-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
45-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
46-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
47-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
48-  | not (b : Bexp)
49-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
50-
51---  In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete
52---  syntax* that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax
53---  trees -- the process that, for example, would translate the string
54---  `"1 + 2 * 3"` to the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
55-
56---  For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
57---  defining the same abstract syntax:
58-
59---  a ::= nat
60---      | a + a
61---      | a − a
62---      | a * a
63---  b ::= bool
64---      | a = a
65---      | a ≠ a
66---      | a ≤ a
67---      | a > a
68---      | ¬ b
69---      | b ∧ b
70-
71---  Compared to the Lean version above...
72-
73---  - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions
74---    about the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the
75---    addition operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other
76---    aspects of lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence
77---    of `+`, `-`, and `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions,
78---    etc.) unspecified. Some additional information -- and human
79---    intelligence -- would be required to turn this description into a
80---    formal definition, e.g., for implementing a compiler. The Lean
81---    version consistently omits all this information and concentrates on
82---    the abstract syntax only.
83-
84---  - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its
85---    informality makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like
86---    discussions at the blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more
87---    important than nailing down every detail precisely.
88-
89---    Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch
90---    freely among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of
91---    BNF they're using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready
92---    informal understanding is all that's important.
93-
94---  It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones
95---  for communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
96---  implementations and proofs.
97-
98---  ### Evaluation
99-
100---  *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
101-
102-namespace Aexp
103-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
104-  match a with
105-  | num   n     =>  n
106-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
107-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
108-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
109-
110-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
111-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
112-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
113-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
114-
115-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
116-end Aexp
117-
118---  Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean.
119-
120-namespace Bexp
121-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
122-  match b with
123-  | bool b     =>  b
124-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
125-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
126-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
127-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
128-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
129-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
130-
131-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
132-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
133-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
134-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
135-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
136-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
137-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
138-end Bexp
139-
140---  It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
141---  `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
142---  `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe
143---  the call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and
144---  `Bexp.eval_gt`.
145-
146---  _Quiz:_
147-
148---  What does the following expression evaluate to?
149-
150---  Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
151-
152---  (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
153-
154---  ### Optimization
155-
156---  We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose
157---  we define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
158---  simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
159---  `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
160-
161-namespace Aexp
162-
163-def optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
164-  match a with
165-  | num   n          => num n
166-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
167-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
168-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
169-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
170-
171---  To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing, we
172---  can test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
173-
174-example :
175-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
176-                               (.plus (.num 0)
177-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
178-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
179-
180---  But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that
181---  evaluating an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as
182---  the original -- we should prove it!
183-
184---  Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
185---  interesting case is `Aexp.plus`: because `Aexp.optimize0plus` treats
186---  `plus (num 0) e` specially, we case-split on the left operand `a₁` --
187---  and, when it is a numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line
188---  the proof up with the function's own branches. Once the constructors
189---  are exposed, each case is discharged by essentially the same
190---  incantation: unfold `Aexp.optimize0plus`, rewrite `Aexp.eval` by its
191---  characterizing lemmas, then finish with the induction hypotheses.
192---  Notice how repetitive that makes the proof.

194-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
195-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
196-  induction a with
197-  | num n => rfl
198-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
199-    cases a₁ with
200-    | num n =>
201-      cases n with
202-      | zero =>
203-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
204-        exact ih₂
205-      | succ n =>
206-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num]
207-        rw [ih₂]
208-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
209-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
210-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
211-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
212-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
213-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
214-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
215-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
216-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
217-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
218-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_minus]
219-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
220-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
221-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_mult]
222-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]

224---  We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand --
225---  peeling `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly
226---  the case analysis that `Aexp.optimize0plus` itself performs.

228---  The `fun_induction` tactic inducts along a function's **own** recursion
229---  structure: `fun_induction
230---  Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per
231---  branch of `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch
232---  included -- so the nested `cases` disappear.
233-
234---  Before applying `fun_induction` to a function as complex as
235---  `Aexp.optimize0plus`, let's see how it works on somthing simpler.
236---  Recall the definition of `Nat.even` and `Nat.odd`:
237-
238-def Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
239-  match n with
240-  | 0 => true
241-  | 1 => false
242-  | n' + 2 => even n'
243-
244-def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := Nat.even (n + 1)
245-
246---  Normally, if we perform induction on `n`, we get two cases - `0` and
247---  `n' + 1` - one for each of the cases in the inductive definition of
248---  natural numbers. Functional induction on `Nat.even`, however, gives us
249---  three cases - `0`, `1`, and `n' + 2` - corresponding to each of the
250---  cases of its definition.
251-
252-example (n : Nat) (h : Nat.even n = true) : Nat.odd n = false := by
253-  fun_induction Nat.even n
254-  . rfl
255-  . contradiction
256-  . simp [Nat.odd, Nat.even] at *
257-    lia

259---  Now let's try using `fun_induction` on `Aexp.optimize0plus`. When we do
260---  this, every goal has the same shape, so we can attack them uniformly
261---  with the `<;>` combinator and a single tactic, `simp_all`, which
262---  rewrites `Aexp.eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses
263---  the induction hypotheses -- which it picks up from the local context
264---  automatically -- to close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two
265---  lines.

267-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
268-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
269-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
270-
271-end Aexp

315---  ## Evaluation as a Relation
316-
317---  We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
318---  recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often
319---  more flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their
320---  values. This perspective leads to inductive definitions like the
321---  following.
322-
323-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
324-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
325-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
326-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
327-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
328-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
329-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
330-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
331-
332---  One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
333---  presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for
334---  the premises.
335-
336-namespace ArithUnnamed
337-
338-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
339-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
340-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
341-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
342-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
343-
344-end ArithUnnamed
345-
346---  The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives
347---  less control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the
348---  relation. For this reason we adopt the named style.
349-
350---  It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
351---  write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
352---  `n`. The `⇓` symbol is typed `\Downarrow`.
353-
354-namespace Aexp
355-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => EvalR e n
356-
357---  The `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped`
358---  keyword allows us to scope the notation to the `Aexp` namespace so it
359---  doesn't collide with other notations we use for different evaluation
360---  relations later.
361-
362---  ### Inference Rule Notation
363-
364---  In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
365---  `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form
366---  of *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the
367---  conclusion below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be
368---  written like this as an inference rule:
369-
370---  a₁ ⇓ n₁
371---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
372---                      ------------------          (plus)
373---                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
374-
375---  Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version
376---  of the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
377-
378---  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
379---          EvalR a₁ n₁ →
380---          EvalR a₂ n₂ →
381---          EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
382-
383---  Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
384---  informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the
385---  right as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks
386---  between the premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as
387---  `→`. All the variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are
388---  implicitly bound by universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such
389---  variables are often called *metavariables* to distinguish them from the
390---  variables of whatever language we are defining. At the moment, our
391---  arithmetic expressions don't include variables, but we'll soon be
392---  adding them.) The whole collection of rules is understood as being
393---  wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In informal prose,
394---  this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let `Aexp.EvalR`
395---  be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
396-
397---  To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single
398---  inductive definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor
399---  name; above the line are the premises, below the line the conclusion;
400---  metavariables like `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified.
401---  The whole collection of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation
402---  closed under them:
403-
404---  ---------                (num)
405---                          num n ⇓ n
406-
407---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
408---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
409---                      ------------------           (plus)
410---                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
411-
412---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
413---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
414---                     -------------------           (minus)
415---                     minus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ - n₂
416-
417---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
418---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
419---                      ------------------           (mult)
420---                      mult a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁*n₂
421-
422---  _Quiz:_
423-
424---  Which rules are needed to prove the following?
425-
426---  .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
427-
428---  (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult` (D) `mult` and
429---  `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`

446---      match b with
447---      | bool b     => b
448---      | eq   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval == a₂.eval
449---      | neq  a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval != a₂.eval
450---      | le   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
451---      | gt   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval > a₂.eval

459-
460---                    -------------                (bool)

462-
463---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
464---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
465---                    ---------------------        (eq)
466---                    eq a₁ a₂ ⇓ (n₁ == n₂)
467-
468---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁

470---                  ---------------------          (neq)
471---                   neq a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ != n₂
472-
473---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
474---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
475---                    --------------------------   (le)
476---                    le a₁ a₂ ⇓ (Nat.ble n₁ n₂)
477-

482-
483---                           b ⇓ bv
484---                       -----------               (not)
485---                       not b ⇓ !bv
486-
487---                          b₁ ⇓ bv₁
488---                          b₂ ⇓ bv₂
489---                   ----------------------        (and)

492---  ### Equivalence of the Definitions
493-
494---  It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
495---  definitions of evaluation agree.
496-
497-theorem evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
498-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
499-  constructor
500-  · intro h
501-    induction h with
502-    | num n => rfl
503-    | plus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_plus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
504-    | minus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_minus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
505-    | mult h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_mult]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
506-  · intro h
507-    subst h
508-    induction a with
509-    | num n => exact .num n
510-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .plus ih₁ ih₂
511-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .minus ih₁ ih₂
512-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult ih₁ ih₂
513-
514---  We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we
515---  did in the previous section.
516-
517-theorem evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
518-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
519-  constructor <;> intro h
520-  · induction h <;> simp_all
521-  · subst h
522-    induction a <;> constructor <;> assumption
523-
524-end Aexp

534-inductive EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
535-  | bool (b : Bool) : EvalR (.bool b) b

556---  ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
557-
558---  For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean
559---  expressions, the choice of whether to use functional or relational
560---  definitions is mainly a matter of taste. However, there are situations
561---  where relational definitions work much better than functional ones.
562-
563-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
564-
565---  For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
566---  with division:
567-
568-inductive Aexp where
569-  | num (n : Nat)
570-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
571-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
572-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
573-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
574-
575---  Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation
576---  would not be straightforward due to division being a *partial*
577---  operation; i.e., what should we return as the result of
578---  `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One option would be to lift the definition of
579---  `Aexp.eval` to return an option:
580-
581-namespace Aexp
582-
583-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
584-  match a with
585-  | num   n     =>  some n
586-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
587-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
588-                    | _, _ => none
589-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
590-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
591-                    | _, _ => none
592-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
593-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
594-                    | _, _ => none
595-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
596-                    | _, some 0 => none
597-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => if n₂ ∣ n₁ then some (n₁ / n₂) else none
598-                    | _, _ => none
599-end Aexp
600-
601---  This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier version. There are
602---  tools to reduce this overhead, namely monads, but we will not discuss
603---  these in Software Foundations in Lean. Curious readers can learn more
604---  about them from [Functional Programming in
605---  Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
606-
607---  By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
608---  definition.
609-
610-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
611-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
612-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
613-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
614-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
615-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
616-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
617-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
618-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
619-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
620-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
621-
622---  Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
623---  this relation does not specify an output.
624-
625-end Slang.AevalRDivision
626-
627-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
628-
629---  As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
630---  operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
631---  evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
632---  *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results
633---  are *possible*.)
634-
635-inductive Aexp where
636-  | any                            -- NEW
637-  | num (n : Nat)
638-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
639-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
640-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
641-
642---  Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now
643---  *not* a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but
644---  extending the relation is no problem.
645-
646-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
647-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
648-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
649-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
650-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
651-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
652-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
653-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
654-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
655-
656-end Slang.AevalRExtended
657-
658---  At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use
659---  by default?
660-
661---  Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
662---  definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable,
663---  relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand,
664---  and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles from them.
665---  On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
666---  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
667---  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
668---  simplify them during proofs.
669-
670---  In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both*
671---  styles plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to
672---  switch between points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
673---  `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
674-

51---  ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
52-
53---  The evaluators we saw for Slang were formulated in a "big-step" style:
54---  they specify how a given expression can be evaluated to its final value
55---  "all in one big step":
56-
57---  2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
58-
59---  This style is simple and natural for many purposes — indeed, Gilles
60---  Kahn, who popularized it, called it *natural semantics*. But there are
61---  some things it does not do well. In particular, it does not give us a
62---  convenient way of talking about *concurrent* programming languages,
63---  where the semantics of a program — the essence of how it behaves —
64---  includes not just which input states get mapped to which output states,
65---  but also the intermediate states that it passes through along the way;
66---  this is crucial, since these states can also be observed by
67---  concurrently executing code.
68-
69---  Another shortcoming of the big-step style is more technical but equally
70---  critical in many situations. Suppose we want to define a variant of our
71---  expression language where a value could be *either* a number *or* a
72---  list of numbers. In the syntax of this extended language, it will be
73---  possible to write strange expressions like `2 + nil`, and our semantics
74---  for arithmetic expressions will then need to say something about how
75---  such expressions behave. One possibility is to maintain the convention
76---  that every arithmetic expression evaluates to some number by choosing
77---  some way of viewing a list as a number — e.g., by specifying that a
78---  list should be interpreted as `0` when it occurs in a context expecting
79---  a number. But this would be a bit of a hack.
80-
81---  A much more natural approach is simply to say that the behavior of the
82---  expression `2 + nil` is *undefined* — i.e., it doesn't evaluate to any
83---  result at all. And we can easily do this: we just have to formulate
84---  `aeval` and `beval` as inductive propositions rather than functions, so
85---  that we can make them partial functions instead of total ones.
86-
87---  Now, however, we encounter a subtlety that will become important once
88---  we move to a full programming language with looping. There, a program
89---  might fail to produce a result for *two quite different reasons*:
90---  either because the execution gets into an infinite loop or because, at
91---  some point, the program tries to do an operation that makes no sense,
92---  such as adding a number to a list, so that none of the evaluation rules
93---  can be applied.
94-
95---  These two outcomes — nontermination vs. getting stuck in an erroneous
96---  configuration — should not be confused. In particular, we want to
97---  *allow* the first (because permitting the possibility of infinite loops
98---  is the price we pay for the convenience of programming with general
99---  looping constructs) but *prevent* the second (which is just wrong), for
100---  example by adding some form of *typechecking* to the language. Indeed,
101---  this will be a major topic of the next chapter, on *types*. As a first
102---  step, we need a way of presenting the semantics that allows us to
103---  distinguish nontermination from erroneous "stuck states."
104-
105---  So, for lots of reasons, we'd like to have a finer-grained way of
106---  defining and reasoning about program behaviors. This is the topic of
107---  the present chapter. Our goal is to replace the "big-step" `Eval`
108---  relation with a "small-step" relation that specifies, for a given
109---  program, how its atomic steps of computation are performed. In the
110---  *small-step* style, we show how to "reduce" an expression to a simpler
111---  form by performing a single step of computation:
112-
113---  2 + 2 + 3 * 4
114---  ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
115---  ⟶ 4 + 12
116---  ⟶ 16
117-
118---  ## A Toy Language
119-
120---  To save space, we start with an incredibly simple language of just
121---  constants and addition. (We use single-letter constructors `c` and `p`
122---  — for Constant and Plus — for brevity.) The same techniques scale up to
123---  richer languages.
124-
125-inductive Tm where
126-  | c (n : Nat)          -- Constant
127-  | p (t₁ t₂ : Tm)       -- Plus
128-
129---  A standard big-step evaluator, as a function.
130-
131-def evalF (t : Tm) : Nat :=
132-  match t with
133-  | .c n => n
134-  | .p t₁ t₂ => evalF t₁ + evalF t₂
135-
136---  Here is the same evaluator, written in exactly the same style, but
137---  formulated as an inductively defined relation. We use the notation
138---  `t ⇓ n` for "`t` evaluates to `n`."
139-
140---  The `notation` command below is how that is declared: it introduces `⇓`
141---  as infix syntax for the `Eval` relation defined with it, with a
142---  precedence saying how tightly it binds. This is the lightweight way to
143---  name a relation; later chapters, where a whole object language needs a
144---  grammar rather than a single operator, reach for `declare_syntax_cat`
145---  instead.
146-
147---  -------                (const)
148---                          c n ⇓ n
149-
150---                          t₁ ⇓ n₁
151---                          t₂ ⇓ n₂
152---                      -----------------          (plus)
153---                      p t₁ t₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
154-
155-inductive Eval : Tm → Nat → Prop where
156-  | const (n : Nat) : Eval (.c n) n
157-  | plus (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : Eval t₁ n₁) (h₂ : Eval t₂ n₂) : Eval (.p t₁ t₂) (n₁ + n₂)
158-
159-notation:50 t " ⇓ " n => Eval t n
160-
161---  Now, here is the corresponding *small-step* relation, written `t ⟶ t'`:
162-
163---  -------------------------------      (plus)
164---                  p (c n₁) (c n₂) ⟶ c (n₁ + n₂)
165-
166---                           t₁ ⟶ t₁'
167---                      --------------------             (plusLeft)
168---                      p t₁ t₂ ⟶ p t₁' t₂
169-
170---                           t₂ ⟶ t₂'
171---                   ----------------------------        (plusRight)
172---                   p (c n₁) t₂ ⟶ p (c n₁) t₂'
173-
174-namespace SimpleArith1
175-
176-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
177-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
178-      Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
179-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm)
180-      (h : Step t₁ t₁') :
181-      Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
182-  | plusRight (n₁ : Nat) (t₂ t₂' : Tm)
183-      (h : Step t₂ t₂') :
184-      Step (.p (.c n₁) t₂) (.p (.c n₁) t₂')
185-
186-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
187-
188---  Things to notice:
189-
190---  - We are defining a single reduction step, in which just one `p` node
191---    is replaced by its value.
192-
193---  - Each step finds the *leftmost* `p` node that is ready to go (both of
194---    its operands are constants) and rewrites it in place. The first rule
195---    tells how to rewrite this `p` node itself; the other two rules tell
196---    how to find it.
197-
198---  - A term that is just a constant cannot take a step.
199-
200---  Let's pause and check a couple of examples of reasoning with the step
201---  relation.
202-
203---  If `t₁` steps to `t₁'`, then `p t₁ t₂` steps to `p t₁' t₂`.
204-
205-example :
206-    (.p
207-      (.p (.c 1) (.c 3))
208-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶
209-    (.p
210-      (.c 4)
211-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) := by
212-  apply Step.plusLeft; apply Step.plus
213-
214---  ### Exercise (1 star): test_step_2 ⭐
215-
216---  Right-hand sides step only once the left side is a value.
217-
218-example :
219-    (.p
220-      (.c 0)
221-      (.p
222-        (.c 2)
223-        (.p
224-          (.c 1)
225-          (.c 3))))
226-      ⟶
227-    (.p
228-      (.c 0)
229-      (.p
230-        (.c 2)
231-        (.c 4))) := by
232-  apply Step.plusRight; apply Step.plusRight; apply Step.plus
233-
234---  _Quiz:_
235-
236---  To what does the following term step?
237-
238---  .p
239---    (.p
240---      (.c 1)
241---      (.c 2))
242---    (.p
243---      (.c 1)
244---      (.c 2))
245-
246---  (A) `.c 6` (B) `.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2))` (C)
247---  `.p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)` (D) `.p (.c 3) (.c 3)` (E) None of the
248---  above
249-
250---  _Quiz:_
251-
252---  What about this one?
253-
254---  .c 1
255-
256---  (A) `.c 1` (B) `.p (.c 0) (.c 1)` (C) None of the above
257-
258-end SimpleArith1
259-
260---  ## Relations
261-
262---  We will be working with several different single-step relations, so it
263---  is helpful to generalize a bit and state a few definitions and theorems
264---  about relations in general. (The optional chapter `Rel` in *Logical
265---  Foundations* develops some of these ideas in a bit more detail;
266---  reviewing that chapter may be useful if the treatment here feels too
267---  terse.)
268-
269---  A *binary relation* on a type `X` is a family of propositions
270---  parameterized by two elements of `X` — i.e., a proposition about pairs
271---  of elements of `X`.
272-
273---  Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
274---      Should we be getting this (and `Deterministic`, `Multi`, etc. if
275---      appropriate) from the Lean standard library? If not, should we
276---      match the concepts in CSLib, if they exists there?
277-
278-def Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
279-
280---  Our main examples of such relations in this chapter will be the
281---  single-step reduction relation, `⟶`, and its multi-step variant, `⟶*`,
282---  defined below, but there are many other examples — e.g., the "equals,"
283---  "less than," "less than or equal to," and "is the square of" relations
284---  on numbers, and the "prefix of" relation on lists and strings.
285-
286---  One simple property a relation may have is being *deterministic*: like
287---  Slang's big-step evaluation, each element is related to at most one
288---  other.
289-
290---  *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that `t` steps
291---  to `t'`. We prove it by induction on the derivation of the first step.
292-
293---  *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y₁` and `y₂`, then
294---  `y₁` and `y₂` are equal, by induction on a derivation of `x ⟶ y₁`.
295---  There are several cases, depending on the last rule used in this
296---  derivation and the last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y₂`.
297-
298---  - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
299-
300---  - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight`
301---    follow by the induction hypothesis.
302-
303---  - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
304---    `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
305---    `p t₁ t₂` where both `t₁` and `t₂` are constants (by `plus`) *and*
306---    one of `t₁` or `t₂` has the form `p _`.
307-
308---  - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
309---    `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂`
310---    where `t₁` has both the form `p t₁₁ t₁₂` and the form `c n`.
311-
312---  Formally,
313-
314-def Deterministic {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
315-  ∀ x y₁ y₂ : X, R x y₁ → R x y₂ → y₁ = y₂
316-
317-namespace SimpleArith2
318-
319-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic SimpleArith1.Step := by
320-  intro x y₁ y₂ h₁
321-  induction h₁ generalizing y₂ with
322-  | plus n₁ n₂ =>
323-      intro h₂
324-      cases h₂ <;> first | rfl | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _›
325-  | plusLeft t₁ t₁' t₂ hs ih =>
326-      intro h₂
327-      cases h₂ <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t₁ _›]
328-  | plusRight n₁ t₂ t₂' hs ih =>
329-      intro h₂
330-      cases h₂ <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t₂ _›]
331-
332-end SimpleArith2
333-
334---  Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
335---      In the Rocq there is the development of a special tactic to make
336---      this proof simpler. Do we want that here?
337-
338---  ### Values
339-
340---  Next, it will be useful to slightly reformulate the definition of
341---  single-step reduction by stating it in terms of "values."
342-
343---  It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract
344---  machine*:
345-
346---  - At any moment, the *state* of the machine is a term.
347-
348---  - A *step* of the machine is an atomic unit of computation — here, a
349---    single "add" operation.
350-
351---  - The *halting states* of the machine are ones where there is no more
352---    computation to be done.
353-
354---  We can then *execute* a term `t` as follows:
355-
356---  - Take `t` as the starting state of the machine.
357-
358---  - Repeatedly use the `⟶` relation to find a sequence of machine states,
359---    starting with `t`, where each state steps to the next.
360-
361---  - When no more reduction is possible, "read out" the final state of the
362---    machine as the result of execution.
363-
364---  Intuitively, it is clear that the final states of our machine are
365---  always terms of the form `c n` for some `n`. We call such terms
366---  *values*.
367-
368-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
369-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
370-
371---  Having introduced the idea of values, we can use it in the definition
372---  of the `⟶` relation to write the `plusRight` rule in a slightly more
373---  elegant way.
374-
375---  ------------------------------      (plus)
376---                  p (c n₁) (c n₂) ⟶ c (n₁ + n₂)
377-
378---                           t₁ ⟶ t₁'
379---                      -------------------             (plusLeft)
380---                      p t₁ t₂ ⟶ p t₁' t₂
381-
382---                           IsValue v₁
383---                           t₂ ⟶ t₂'
384---                      -------------------             (plusRight)
385---                      p v₁ t₂ ⟶ p v₁ t₂'
386-
387---  Again, the variable names in the informal presentation carry important
388---  information: by convention, `v₁` ranges only over values, while `t₁`
389---  and `t₂` range over arbitrary terms.
390-
391---  (Given this convention, the explicit `IsValue` hypothesis is arguably
392---  redundant, since the naming convention tells us where to add it when
393---  translating the informal rule to Lean. We'll keep it for now, to
394---  maintain a close correspondence between the informal and Lean versions
395---  of the rules, but later on we'll drop it in informal rules for
396---  brevity.)
397-
398---  Here are the formal rules.
399-
400-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
401-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
402-      Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
403-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm)
404-      (h : Step t₁ t₁') :
405-      Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
406-  | plusRight (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm)
407-      (hv : IsValue v₁)
408-      (h : Step t₂ t₂') :
409-      Step (.p v₁ t₂) (.p v₁ t₂')
410-
411-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
412-
413---  ### Exercise (3 stars): redo_determinism ⭐⭐⭐
414-
415---  As a sanity check on this change, let's re-verify determinism. Here's
416---  an informal proof:
417-
418---  *Proof sketch*: We must show that if `x` steps to both `y₁` and `y₂`,
419---  then `y₁` and `y₂` are equal. Consider the final rules used in the
420---  derivations of `x ⟶ y₁` and `x ⟶ y₂`.
421-
422---  - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
423-
424---  - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight`
425---    follow by the induction hypothesis.
426-
427---  - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
428---    `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
429---    `p t₁ t₂` where both `t₁` and `t₂` are constants (by `plus`) *and*
430---    one of `t₁` or `t₂` has the form `p _`.
431-
432---  - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
433---    `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂`
434---    where `t₁` both has the form `p t₁₁ t₁₂` and is a value (hence has
435---    the form `c n`).
436-
437---  Most of this proof is the same as the one above. But to get maximum
438---  benefit from the exercise you should try to write your formal version
439---  from scratch and just use the earlier one if you get stuck. The
440---  impossible cross-cases now also use the fact that a `IsValue` (a `c n`)
441---  cannot step.
442-
443-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Step := by
444-  intro x y₁ y₂ h₁
445-  induction h₁ generalizing y₂ with
446-  | plus n₁ n₂ =>
447-      intro h₂; cases h₂ with
448-      | plus => rfl
449-      | plusLeft _ _ _ hs => cases hs
450-      | plusRight _ _ _ _ hs => cases hs
451-  | plusLeft t₁ t₁' t₂ hs ih =>
452-      intro h₂; cases h₂ with
453-      | plus => cases hs
454-      | plusLeft _ _ _ hs₂ => rw [ih _ hs₂]
455-      | plusRight _ _ _ hv hs₂ => cases hv; cases hs
456-  | plusRight v₁ t₂ t₂' hv hs ih =>
457-      intro h₂; cases h₂ with
458-      | plus => cases hs
459-      | plusLeft _ _ _ hs₂ => cases hv; cases hs₂
460-      | plusRight _ _ _ _ hs₂ => rw [ih _ hs₂]
461-
462---  ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
463-
464---  The definition of single-step reduction for our toy language is fairly
465---  simple, but for a larger language it would be easy to forget one of the
466---  rules and accidentally create a situation where some term cannot take a
467---  step even though it has not been completely reduced to a value. The
468---  following theorem shows that we did not, in fact, make such a mistake
469---  here.
470-
471---  *Theorem* (*Strong Progress*): If `t` is a term, then either `t` is a
472---  value or else there exists a term `t'` such that `t ⟶ t'`.
473-
474---  *Proof*: By induction on `t`.
475-
476---  - Suppose `t = c n`. Then `t` is a value.
477-
478---  - Suppose `t = p t₁ t₂`, where (by the IH) `t₁` either is a value or
479---    can step to some `t₁'`, and where `t₂` is either a value or can step
480---    to some `t₂'`. We must show `p t₁ t₂` is either a value or steps to
481---    some `t'`.
482-
483---    - If `t₁` and `t₂` are both values, then `t` can take a step, by
484---      `plus`.
485-
486---    - If `t₁` is a value and `t₂` can take a step, then so can `t`, by
487---      `plusRight`.
488-
489---    - If `t₁` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `plusLeft`.
490-
491---  Or, formally:
492-
493-theorem strong_progress (t : Tm) : IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
494-  induction t with
495-  | c n => left; exact .const n
496-  | p t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
497-      right
498-      cases ih₁ with
499-      | inl hv₁ =>
500-          cases ih₂ with
501-          | inl hv₂ =>
502-              cases hv₁ with
503-              | const n₁ =>
504-                  cases hv₂ with
505-                  | const n₂ => exact ⟨.c (n₁ + n₂), .plus n₁ n₂⟩
506-          | inr h₂ =>
507-              obtain ⟨t₂', ht₂⟩ := h₂
508-              exact ⟨.p t₁ t₂', .plusRight t₁ t₂ t₂' hv₁ ht₂⟩
509-      | inr h₁ =>
510-          obtain ⟨t₁', ht₁⟩ := h₁
511-          exact ⟨.p t₁' t₂, .plusLeft t₁ t₁' t₂ ht₁⟩
512-
513---  This important property is called *strong progress*, because every term
514---  either is a value or can "make progress" by stepping to some other
515---  term. (The qualifier "strong" distinguishes it from a more refined
516---  version that we'll see in later chapters, called simply *progress*.)
517-
518---  The idea of "making progress" can be extended to tell us something
519---  interesting about values in this language: they are exactly the terms
520---  that do *not* make progress in this sense. Let's give a name to "terms
521---  that cannot make progress." We'll call them *normal forms*.
522-
523-def IsNormalForm {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t : X) : Prop :=
524-  ¬ ∃ t', R t t'
525-
526---  Note that this definition specifies what it is to be a normal form for
527---  an *arbitrary* relation `R` over an arbitrary type `X`, not just for

680---  ## Multi-Step Reduction
681-
682---  We've been working so far with the *single-step reduction* relation
683---  `⟶`, which formalizes the individual steps of an abstract machine for
684---  executing programs. We can use the same machine to reduce programs to
685---  completion — to find out what final result they yield. This can be
686---  formalized as follows:
687-
688---  - First, we define a *multi-step reduction relation* `⟶*`, which
689---    relates terms `t` and `t'` if `t` can reach `t'` by any number
690---    (including zero) of single reduction steps.
691-
692---  - Then we define a "result" of a term `t` as a normal form that `t` can
693---    reach by multi-step reduction.
694-
695---  Since we'll want to reuse the idea of multi-step reduction many times
696---  with many different single-step relations, let's define the concept
697---  generically. Given a relation `R` (e.g., the step relation `⟶`), we
698---  define a new relation `Multi R`, called the *multi-step closure of
699---  `R`*, as follows.
700-
701-inductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
702-  | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
703-  | step (x y z : X) (h₁ : R x y) (h₂ : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z
704-
705---  Note to developers (berberman):
706---      I would make some arguments implicit to proivde a cleaner interface
707---      (FYI the [mathlib
708---      version](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Logic/Relation.html#Relation.ReflTransGen))
709-
710---  The effect of this definition is that `Multi R` relates two elements
711---  `x` and `y` if
712-
713---  - `x = y`, or
714-
715---  - `R x y`, or
716-
717---  - there is some nonempty sequence `z₁`, `z₂` , ..., `zₙ` such that
718-
719---    `R x₁ z₁,
720---    R z₁ z₂,
721---    ...,
722---    R zₙ y.`
723-
724---  Intuitively, if `R` describes a single-step of computation, then
725---  `z₁ ... zₙ` are the intermediate steps of computation that get us from
726---  `x` to `y`.
727-
728---  We write `⟶*` for the `Multi Step` relation on terms
729-
730-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
731-
732---  The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
733-
734---  First, it is obviously *reflexive* (a term can execute to itself by
735---  taking zero steps). That is just what the `Multi.refl` constructor
736---  says, so such a goal can always be closed with `exact .refl _`. It
737---  comes up often enough that it is worth registering the constructor as a
738---  *reflexivity lemma*, with the `@[refl]` attribute. The `rfl` tactic
739---  then closes a zero-step execution exactly as it closes `x = x`:
740-
741-attribute [refl] Multi.refl
742-
743-example : (.c 5 : Tm) ⟶* .c 5 := by rfl
744-
745---  This pays off at the *end* of a reduction sequence too: the final
746---  `Multi.step` leaves a goal relating a term to itself, which `rfl`
747---  discharges.
748-
749-example : (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) ⟶* .c (1 + 2) := by
750-  apply Multi.step (y := .c (1 + 2))
751-  · exact .plus 1 2
752-  · rfl
753-
754---  Second, it *contains* `R` — single-step reductions are a particular
755---  case of multi-step executions. (It is this fact that justifies the word
756---  "closure" in "multi-step closure of `R`.")
757-
758-theorem multi_single {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y : X) (h : R x y) :
759-    Multi R x y :=
760-  .step x y y h (.refl y)
761-
762---  Third, `Multi R` is *transitive*.
763-
764-theorem multi_trans {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y z : X)
765-    (g : Multi R x y) (h : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z := by
766-  induction g with
767-  | refl a => exact h
768-  | step a b c h₁ h₂ ih => exact .step a b z h₁ (ih h)
769-
770---  In particular, for the `Multi Step` relation on terms, if `t₁ ⟶* t₂`
771---  and `t₂ ⟶* t₃`, then `t₁ ⟶* t₃`.
772-
773---  _Quiz:_
774-
775---  Which of the following relations on numbers *cannot* be expressed as
776---  `Multi R` for some `R`?
777-
778---  (A) less than or equal (B) strictly less than (C) equal (D) none of the
779---  above
780-

785-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4)))
786-  · exact .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 0 3)
787-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.c (2 + 4)))
788-  · exact .plusRight _ _ _ (.const _) (.plus 2 4)
789-  · exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus (0 + 3) (2 + 4))

820---  ### Normal Forms Again
821-
822---  If `t` reduces to `t'` in zero or more steps and `t'` is a normal form,
823---  we say that "`t'` is *a normal form of* `t`."
824-
825-def IsNormalFormOf {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t t' : X) : Prop :=
826-  Multi R t t' ∧ IsNormalForm R t'
827-
828---  We have already seen that, for our language, single-step reduction is
829---  deterministic — i.e., a given term can take a single step in at most
830---  one way. It follows that, if `t` can reach a normal form, then this
831---  normal form is unique.
832-
833---  In other words, we can actually pronounce `IsNormalFormOf t t'` as
834---  "`t'` is *the* normal form of `t`."
835-
836---  ### Exercise (3 stars): normal_forms_unique (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
837-
838-theorem normal_forms_unique : Deterministic (IsNormalFormOf Step) := by
839-  -- We recommend using this initial setup as-is!
840-  intro x y₁ y₂ p₁ p₂
841-  obtain ⟨p₁₁, p₁₂⟩ := p₁
842-  obtain ⟨p₂₁, p₂₂⟩ := p₂
843-  induction p₁₁ generalizing y₂ with
844-  | refl a =>
845-      cases p₂₁ with
846-      | refl => rfl
847-      | step _ b _ h₁ _ => exact absurd ⟨b, h₁⟩ p₁₂
848-  | step a b c h₁ h₂ ih =>
849-      cases p₂₁ with
850-      | refl => exact absurd ⟨b, h₁⟩ p₂₂
851-      | step _ b' _ h₁' h₂' =>
852-          have hbb : b = b' := step_deterministic _ _ _ h₁ h₁'
853-          subst hbb
854-          exact ih y₂ p₁₂ h₂' p₂₂
855-
856---  Indeed, something stronger is true for this language (though not for
857---  all the languages we will see): the reduction of *any* term `t` will
858---  eventually reach a normal form in a finite number of steps — i.e.,
859---  `IsNormalFormOf` is a *total* function. We say the `Step` relation is
860---  *normalizing*. To prove it, we need a couple of congruence lemmas.
861-
862-def Normalizing {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
863-  ∀ t, ∃ t', IsNormalFormOf R t t'
864-
865-theorem multistep_congr_1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶* t₁') : (.p t₁ t₂) ⟶* (.p t₁' t₂) := by
866-  induction h with
867-  | refl x => exact .refl _
868-  | step x y z h₁ h₂ ih => exact .step _ (.p y t₂) _ (.plusLeft x y t₂ h₁) ih
869-
870---  ### Exercise (2 stars): multistep_congr_2 ⭐⭐
871-
872-theorem multistep_congr_2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v₁) (h : t₂ ⟶* t₂') :
873-    (.p v₁ t₂) ⟶* (.p v₁ t₂') := by
874-  induction h with
875-  | refl x => exact .refl _
876-  | step x y z h₁ h₂ ih => exact .step _ (.p v₁ y) _ (.plusRight v₁ x y hv h₁) ih
877-
878---  With these lemmas in hand, the main proof is a straightforward
879---  induction.
880-
881---  *Theorem*: The `Step` relation is normalizing — i.e., for every `t`
882---  there exists some `t'` such that `t` reduces to `t'` and `t'` is a
883---  normal form.
884-
885---  *Proof sketch*: By induction on terms. There are two cases:
886-
887---  - `t = c n` for some `n`. Here `t` doesn't take a step, and we have
888---    `t' = t`. We derive the left-hand side by reflexivity and the
889---    right-hand side by observing (a) that values are normal forms (by
890---    `nf_same_as_value`) and (b) that `t` is a value (by `const`).
891-
892---  - `t = p t₁ t₂` for some `t₁` and `t₂`. By the IH, `t₁` and `t₂` reduce
893---    to normal forms `t₁'` and `t₂'`. Recall that normal forms are values
894---    (by `nf_same_as_value`); we therefore know that `t₁' = c n₁` and
895---    `t₂' = c n₂` for some `n₁` and `n₂`. We combine the `⟶*` derivations
896---    for `t₁` and `t₂` using `multistep_congr_1` and `multistep_congr_2`
897---    to prove that `p t₁ t₂` reduces in many steps to `t' = c (n₁ + n₂)`.
898---    Finally, `c (n₁ + n₂)` is a value, which is in turn a normal form.
899-
900-theorem step_normalizing : Normalizing Step := by
901-  intro t
902-  induction t with
903-  | c n => exact ⟨.c n, .refl _, (nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const n)⟩
904-  | p t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
905-      obtain ⟨t₁', hs₁, hnf₁⟩ := ih₁
906-      obtain ⟨t₂', hs₂, hnf₂⟩ := ih₂
907-      obtain ⟨n₁⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf₁
908-      obtain ⟨n₂⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf₂
909-      apply Exists.intro (.c (n₁ + n₂))
910-      apply And.intro _ ((nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const _))
911-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t₁ (.c n₁) t₂ hs₁)
912-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n₁) t₂ (.c n₂) (.const n₁) hs₂)
913-      exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n₁ n₂)

915---  ### Equivalence of Big-Step and Small-Step
916-
917---  Having defined the operational semantics of our tiny programming
918---  language in two different ways (big-step and small-step), it makes
919---  sense to ask whether these definitions actually define the same thing!
920-
921---  They do, though it takes a little work to show it. The details are left
922---  as an exercise. We consider the two implications separately. First,
923---  big-step evaluation implies multi-step reduction to a value.
924-
925---  ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval ⭐⭐⭐
926-
927-theorem multistep_of_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) (h : t ⇓ n) : t ⟶* .c n := by
928-  induction h with
929-  | const n => exact .refl _
930-  | plus t₁ t₂ n₁ n₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
931-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t₁ (.c n₁) t₂ ih₁)
932-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n₁) t₂ (.c n₂) (.const n₁) ih₂)
933-      exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n₁ n₂)
934-
935---  The key ideas in the proof can be seen in the following picture:
936-
937---  p t₁ t₂ ⟶            (by plusLeft)
938---  p t₁' t₂ ⟶           (by plusLeft)
939---  p t₁'' t₂ ⟶          (by plusLeft)
940---  ...
941---  p (c n₁) t₂ ⟶        (by plusRight)
942---  p (c n₁) t₂' ⟶       (by plusRight)
943---  p (c n₁) t₂'' ⟶      (by plusRight)
944---  ...
945---  p (c n₁) (c n₂) ⟶    (by plus)
946---  c (n₁ + n₂)
947-
948---  That is, the multi-step reduction of a term of the form `p t₁ t₂`
949---  proceeds in three phases:
950-
951---  - First, we use `plusLeft` some number of times to reduce `t₁` to a
952---    normal form, which must (by `nf_same_as_value`) be a term of the form
953---    `c n₁` for some `n₁`.
954-
955---  - Next, we use `plusRight` some number of times to reduce `t₂` to a
956---    normal form, which must again be a term of the form `c n₂` for some
957---    `n₂`.
958-
959---  - Finally, we use `plus` one time to reduce `p (c n₁) (c n₂)` to
960---    `c (n₁ + n₂)`.
961-
962---  To formalize this intuition, you'll need the congruence lemmas from
963---  above, plus some basic properties of `⟶*` (that it is reflexive,
964---  transitive, and includes `⟶`).
965-
966---  ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval_inf (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
967-
968---  Write a detailed informal version of the proof of `multistep_of_eval`.
969---  (A paper exercise — there is no Lean proof to fill in here.)
970-
971---  _Theorem_: for all `t`, `n`, if `t ⇓ n` then `t ⟶* c n`.
972-
973---  _Proof_: By induction on a derivation of `t ⇓ n`.
974-
975---    - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `const`.  Then `t = c n`.
976---      We must show `c n ⟶* c n`.  This holds by `refl`.
977-
978---    - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `plus`.  Then
979---      `t = p t₁ t₂`, and we know that `t₁ ⇓ c n₁` and `t₂ ⇓ c n₂` for some
980---      `n₁` and `n₂`, with `n = n₁ + n₂`.  The IH tells us that `t₁ ⟶* c n₁` and
981---      `t₂ ⟶* c n₂`.  We must show that `p t₁ t₂ ⟶* c (n₁ + n₂)`.
982-
983---      First, `p t₁ t₂ ⟶* p (c n₁) t₂` by `multistep_congr_1` and the multistep
984---      derivation for `t₁`.  Observing that `c n₁` is a value, we also have
985---      `p (c n₁) t₂ ⟶* p (c n₁) (c n₂)` by `multistep_congr_2` and the multistep
986---      derivation for `t₂`.  It's also easy to see by `plus` that

1233---  _Quiz:_
1234-
1235---  Which of these properties does this small-step semantics for `Slang`
1236---  expressions satisfy? (Yes or No for each.)
1237-
1238---  - determinism
1239---  - strong progress (every non-value takes a step)
1240---  - values and normal forms coincide (i.e., there are no "stuck" terms)
1241---  - the step relation is normalizing (i.e., evaluation always terminates)
1242-
1243---  Let us make good on the first of those answers. Both step relations are
1244---  *deterministic*: the value guards on the "step the right operand" rules
1245---  mean that at most one rule ever applies to a given term.

1257-    first
1258-      | rfl
1259-      | cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›
1260-      | (cases ‹IsAValue _›; cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›)
1261-      | (congr 1 <;> first | rfl | (apply ‹∀ _, AStep _ _ → _ = _› <;> assumption))

1280---  ### Nondeterministic Evaluation
1281-
1282---  The relation `⟶a` above bakes in a *left-to-right* evaluation order:
1283---  the rule `plusRight` can fire only once the left operand is already a
1284---  value (`IsAValue v₁`). But nothing about the *meaning* of `+` requires
1285---  that order — we could just as well reduce the right operand first, or
1286---  interleave the two. Different orders are exactly what a concurrent or
1287---  optimizing implementation might choose, so it is natural to ask whether
1288---  the choice can affect the final answer.
1289-

1291---  identical to `⟶a` except that we *drop* the `IsAValue` side-condition:
1292---  either operand may take a step at any time.
