1361-  induction h with
1362-  | refl x => exact .refl x
1363-  | step x y z h₁ _ ih => exact .step x y z (astep_imp_anstep x y h₁) ih
1364-
1365---  ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_anstep_agree ⭐⭐⭐
1366-
1367---  Now put the pieces together: prove that the deterministic and
1368---  nondeterministic semantics always compute the *same* final result. That
1369---  is, if `a` fully reduces to `.num n₁` under `⟶a` and to `.num n₂` under
1370---  `⟶n`, then `n₁ = n₂`.
1371-
1372---  *Hint:* both `.num n₁` and `.num n₂` are reachable by `⟶n` (use
1373---  `multi_astep_imp_anstep` for the first), and `⟶n` preserves `eval`.
1374-
1375-theorem astep_anstep_agree (a : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat)
1376-    (hd : Multi AStep a (.num n₁)) (hn : Multi ANStep a (.num n₂)) : n₁ = n₂ := by
1377-  have e₁ := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n₁)
1378-    (multi_astep_imp_anstep a (.num n₁) hd)
1379-  have e₂ := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n₂) hn
1380-  simp only [Aexp.eval] at e₁ e₂
1381-  lia
1382-
1383---  So even though `⟶n` is genuinely nondeterministic, the value it
1384---  eventually produces is completely determined — and it is the same value
1385---  the deterministic machine (and the big-step evaluator) computes. This
1386---  *confluence to a unique result* is exactly the property one wants when
1387---  reordering or parallelizing the evaluation of pure expressions.
1388-
1389---  ### A Small-Step Stack Machine
1390-
1391---  Our last example is a small-step semantics for a *stack machine* that
1392---  evaluates arithmetic expressions. The machine's instructions push a
1393---  constant or combine the top two stack entries. The machine's behavior
1394---  should match the big-step `Aexp.eval` function defined earlier.
1395-
1396---  A *program* is a list of instructions, and the *stack* is a list of
1397---  numbers.
1398-
1399-inductive SInstr where
1400-  | push (n : Nat)
1401-  | plus
1402-  | minus
1403-  | mult
1404-
1405-abbrev Stack := List Nat
1406-abbrev Prog := List SInstr
1407-
1408---  The compiler emits code in the postfix order sketched above:
1409-
1410-def compile : Aexp → Prog
1411-  | .num n => [.push n]
1412-  | .plus a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.plus]
1413-  | .minus a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.minus]
1414-  | .mult a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.mult]
1415-
1416-example : compile (.plus (.num 2) (.num 3)) = [.push 2, .push 3, .plus] := rfl
1417-
1418---  Now the small-step machine itself: each step consumes the next
1419---  instruction and updates the stack.
1420-
1421-inductive StackStep : Prog × Stack → Prog × Stack → Prop where
1422-  | push (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n : Nat) : StackStep (.push n :: p, stk) (p, n :: stk)
1423-  | plus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1424-      StackStep (.plus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m + n) :: stk)
1425-  | minus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1426-      StackStep (.minus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m - n) :: stk)
1427-  | mult (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1428-      StackStep (.mult :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m * n) :: stk)
1429-
1430---  The machine is deterministic:
1431-
1432-theorem stack_step_deterministic : Deterministic StackStep := by
1433-  intro x y₁ y₂ h₁ h₂
1434-  cases h₁ <;> cases h₂ <;> rfl
1435-
1436---  ### Exercise (3 stars): compiler_is_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1437-
1438---  Prove the compiler correct: running the compiled program from the empty
1439---  stack reduces, in some number of steps, to a stack holding exactly the
1440---  value of the expression.
1441-
1442---  *Hint:* this will not go through by a direct induction — the induction
1443---  hypothesis is too weak. Prove a more general statement first, about
1444---  running `compile a` followed by *any* leftover program `p`, starting
1445---  from *any* stack `stk`. (Reassociating the `++`s with
1446---  `List.append_assoc`, and chaining steps with
1447---  `multi_trans`/`multi_single`, are the moves you need.)
1448-
1449-theorem compiler_is_correct (a : Aexp) :
1450-    Multi StackStep (compile a, []) ([], [a.eval]) := by
1451-  have gen : ∀ (a : Aexp) (p : Prog) (stk : Stack),
1452-      Multi StackStep (compile a ++ p, stk) (p, a.eval :: stk) := by
1453-    intro a
1454-    induction a with
1455-    | num n =>
1456-        intro p stk
1457-        simp only [compile, Aexp.eval]
1458-        exact multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.push p stk n)
1459-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1460-        intro p stk
1461-        simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1462-        exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ stk)
1463-          (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₂ _ (a₁.eval :: stk))
1464-            (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.plus p stk a₂.eval a₁.eval)))
1465-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1466-        intro p stk
1467-        simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1468-        exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ stk)
1469-          (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₂ _ (a₁.eval :: stk))
1470-            (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.minus p stk a₂.eval a₁.eval)))
1471-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1472-        intro p stk
1473-        simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1474-        exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ stk)
1475-          (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih₂ _ (a₁.eval :: stk))
1476-            (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.mult p stk a₂.eval a₁.eval)))
1477-  have hfin := gen a [] []
1478-  simp only [List.append_nil] at hfin
1479-  exact hfin
1480-
1481-end Slang
1482-

TS/Stlc.lean

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import LF.Typeclasses
4-import TS.Smallstep
5-
6-import SFLCompat
7-
8---  # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9-
10---  The simply typed lambda-calculus (STLC) is a tiny core calculus
11---  embodying the key concept of *functional abstraction*. This concept
12---  shows up in pretty much every real-world programming language in some
13---  form (functions, procedures, methods, etc.).
14-
15---  We will follow exactly the same pattern as in the previous chapter when
16---  formalizing this calculus (syntax, small-step semantics, typing rules)
17---  and its main properties (progress and preservation). The new technical
18---  challenges arise from the mechanisms of *variable binding* and
19---  *substitution*. It will take some work to deal with these.
20-
21---  The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the famous *lambda
22---  cube* (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which visualizes three sets
23---  of features that can be added to its simple core:
24-
25---  Calculus of Constructions
26---   type operators +--------+
27---                 /|       /|
28---                / |      / |
29---  polymorphism +--------+  |
30---               |  |     |  |
31---               |  +-----|--+
32---               | /      | /
33---               |/       |/
34---               +--------+ dependent types
35---             STLC
36-
37---  Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to adding
38---  *polymorphic types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`. Adding *just*
39---  polymorphism gives us the famous Girard-Reynolds calculus, System F.
40-
41---  Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type operators* like
42---  `List`.
43-
44---  Moving from left to right corresponds to adding *dependent types* like
45---  `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
46-
47---  The top right corner on the back, which combines all three features, is
48---  called the *Calculus of Constructions*. First studied by Coquand and
49---  Huet, it forms the foundation of Lean's logic.
50-
51---  ## Overview
52-
53---  The STLC is built on some collection of *base types*: booleans,
54---  numbers, strings, etc. The exact choice of base types doesn't matter
55---  much — the definition of the language as well as its theoretical
56---  properties work out the same no matter what we choose — so for the sake
57---  of brevity let's take just `Bool` for the moment. In the next chapter
58---  we'll see how to add more base types, and in later chapters we'll
59---  enrich the pure STLC with other useful constructs like pairs, records,
60---  subtyping, and mutable state.
61-
62---  Starting from boolean constants and conditionals, we add three things:
63-
64---  - variables
65---  - function abstractions
66---  - application
67-
68---  This gives us the following collection of abstract syntax constructors
69---  (written out first in informal BNF notation — we'll formalize it below)
70---  for STLC terms `t`.
71-
72---  t ::= x                     (variable)
73---      | λ x : T . t           (abstraction)
74---      | t t                   (application)
75---      | true                  (constant true)
76---      | false                 (constant false)
77---      | if t then t else t    (conditional)
78-
79---  The Greek letter λ ("lambda") in a function abstraction `λx:T. t` is
80---  what gives the calculus its name. The variable `x` is called the
81---  *parameter* to the function; the term `t` is its *body*. The annotation
82---  `:T` specifies the *type* of arguments that the function can be applied
83---  to.
84-
85---  The types of the STLC include `Bool`, which classifies the boolean
86---  constants `true` and `false` as well as more complex computations that
87---  yield booleans, plus *arrow types* that classify functions (as is the
88---  case in Lean).
89-
90---  T ::= Bool
91---      | T → T
92-
93---  Some examples of STLC terms:
94-
95---  `λx:Bool. x`
96-
97---  The identity function for booleans.
98-
99---  `(λx:Bool. x) true`
100-
101---  The identity function for booleans, applied to the boolean `true`.
102-
103---  `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
104-
105---  The boolean "not" function.
106-
107---  `λx:Bool. true`
108-
109---  The constant function that takes every (boolean) argument to `true`.
110-
111---  `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
112-
113---  A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first
114---  one.
115-
116---  (As in Lean, a two-argument function in the lambda-calculus is really a
117---  one-argument function whose body is also a one-argument function.)
118-
119---  `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
120-
121---  A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first
122---  one, applied to the booleans `false` and `true`.
123-
124---  (As in Lean, application associates to the left — i.e., this expression
125---  is parsed as `((λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false) true`.)
126-
127---  `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
128-
129---  A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f` (from booleans to
130---  booleans) as an argument, applies `f` to `true`, and applies `f` again
131---  to the result.
132-
133---  `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
134-
135---  The same higher-order function, applied to the constantly `false`
136---  function.
137-
138---  The last two examples show, the STLC is a language of *higher-order*
139---  functions: we can write down functions that take other functions as
140---  arguments and/or return other functions as results.
141-
142---  The STLC doesn't provide any primitive syntax for defining *named*
143---  functions: i.e., all functions are "anonymous." We'll see in chapter
144---  `MoreStlc` that it is easy to add named functions — indeed, the
145---  fundamental naming and binding mechanisms are exactly the same.
146-
147---  Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
148-
149---  - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
150-
151---  - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
152-
153---  - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type `Bool → Bool`
154-
155---  - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
156-
157---  - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool` (i.e.,
158---    `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
159-
160---  - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
161-
162---  The last two, higher-order examples are left off the list on purpose —
163---  working out their types is the subject of the quizzes that follow.
164-
165---  _Quiz:_
166-
167---  What is the type of the following term?
168-
169---    λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
170-
171---  (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
172-
173---  (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
174-
175---  (C) `Bool → Bool`
176-
177---  (D) `Bool`
178-
179---  (E) none of the above
180-
181---  _Quiz:_
182-
183---  How about the type of this one?
184-
185---    (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
186-
187---  (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
188-
189---  (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
190-
191---  (C) `Bool → Bool`
192-
193---  (D) `Bool`
194-
195---  (E) none of the above
196-
197---  ## Syntax
198-
199---  We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.
200-
201-namespace Stlc
202-
203-open scoped MyGetElem
204-
205---  ### Types
206-
207-inductive Ty where
208-  | bool
209-  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
210-
211---  ### Terms
212-
213-inductive Tm where
214-  | var (x : String)
215-  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
216-  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
217-  | tru
218-  | fls
219-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
220-
221---  We need some notation magic to set up the concrete syntax, as we did in
222---  the Types chapter...
223-
224---  The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both
225---  written inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside
226---  the brackets escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
227-
228---  - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
229-
230---  - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the
231---    brackets is the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>`
232---    is the variable `x`;
233-
234---  - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
235-
236---  Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so
237---  the same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to
238---  typing — for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed
239---  blocks below; nothing later in the chapter depends on it.
240-
241---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: types)
242-
243---  The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→` or `->`,
244---  associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A bare identifier
245---  other than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any
246---  Lean expression of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
247-
248---  To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line to the
249---  category and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is all it takes to add
250---  a new type construct.
251-
252-declare_syntax_cat stlcTy
253-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTy
254-syntax:max "(" stlcTy ")" : stlcTy
255-syntax:max ident : stlcTy
256-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " → " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
257-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " -> " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
258-syntax:max (name := tyBracket) "<{ " stlcTy " }>" : term
259-
260-macro_rules (kind := tyBracket)
261-  | `(<{ ~$T:term }>)    => pure T
262-  | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
263-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
264-      match x.getId.toString with
265-      | "Bool" => `(Ty.bool)
266-      | _ => `(($x : Ty))
267-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>)  => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
268-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
269-
270---  END DETAILS
271-
272---  We'll write types inside of `<{ ... }>` brackets:
273-
274-#check <{ Bool }>
275-#check <{ Bool -> Bool }>
276-#check <{ (Bool -> Bool) -> Bool }>
277-
278---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: terms)
279-
280---  Terms are built from variables, application (associating to the left),
281---  abstraction, the two boolean constants, and conditionals. A binding
282---  occurrence — the `x` in `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own,
283---  `stlcVar`, and `varStr` turns it into the string that `Tm.abs` stores.
284-
285---  Because types and terms share the brackets, each `macro_rules` group
286---  says which bracket it belongs to (`kind := tyBracket`,
287---  `kind := tmBracket`), and each antiquote in a nested quotation says
288---  which grammar it came from. A bare identifier is the one genuinely
289---  overlapping case: `Bool` in term position would otherwise quietly
290---  become a variable named `Bool`, so that rule rejects it, which also
291---  settles which grammar a lone `<{ Bool }>` belongs to.
292-
293---  The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for substitution; we
294---  give it its meaning when we define substitution below. It binds tighter
295---  than application, so `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁`
296---  to `t₂`, and a `λ` or `if` body must be parenthesized:
297---  `[x:=s] (λ y : Bool . x)`.
298-
299-declare_syntax_cat stlcVar
300-syntax:max ident : stlcVar
301-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcVar
302-
303-open Lean in
304-/-- The string named by a variable in binding position. -/
305-def varStr (x : TSyntax `stlcVar) : MacroM Term :=
306-  match x with
307-  | `(stlcVar| $i:ident) => pure (quote i.getId.toString : Term)
308-  | `(stlcVar| ~$e)      => pure e
309-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
310-
311-declare_syntax_cat stlcTm
312-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTm
313-syntax:max "(" stlcTm ")" : stlcTm
314-syntax:max ident : stlcTm
315-syntax:75 stlcTm:75 ppSpace stlcTm:76 : stlcTm
316-syntax:50 "λ " stlcVar " : " stlcTy " . " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
317-syntax:50 "if " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
318-syntax:max "[" stlcVar " := " stlcTm "] " stlcTm:max : stlcTm
319-syntax:max (name := tmBracket) "<{ " stlcTm " }>" : term
320-
321-open Lean in
322-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
323-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
324-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
325-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
326-      match x.getId.toString with
327-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
328-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
329-      | "Bool"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Bool` is a type, not a term"
330-      | _       => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
331-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
332-  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
333-      `(Tm.abs $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
334-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) =>
335-      `(Tm.ite <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
336-
337---  END DETAILS
338-
339---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing it back)
340-
341---  A *delaborator* runs the grammar backwards: it rebuilds the concrete
342---  syntax from a `Ty` or `Tm` value, so that types and terms appearing in
343---  goals and in `#check` output print as `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` rather
344---  than as a pile of constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns it
345---  off, revealing the underlying representation.)
346-
347-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
348-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTy` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
349-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTy]
350-def stlcTy.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
351-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTy true wrapParens prec <|
352-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTy prec
353-where
354-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
355-    let pstx ← `(stlcTy| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
356-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
357-
358-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
359-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
360-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTm]
361-def stlcTm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
362-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTm true wrapParens prec <|
363-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTm prec
364-where
365-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
366-    let pstx ← `(stlcTm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
367-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
368-
369-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
370-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
371-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
372-  let stx ←
373-    match_expr ← getExpr with
374-    | Ty.bool => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
375-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
376-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
377-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
378-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
379-    | _ => do
380-        match ← delab with
381-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
382-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
383-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
384-
385-open Lean in
386-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare identifier in the object syntax? -/
387-def isPlainName (s : String) : Bool :=
388-  !s.isEmpty && s != "_" && !s.front.isDigit &&
389-    s.all fun c => c.isAlphanum || c == '_'
390-
391-open Lean in
392-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
393-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
394-  isPlainName s && s != "true" && s != "false" && s != "Bool"
395-
396-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
397-/-- Rebuild `stlcVar` concrete syntax from the string in a binding position. -/
398-def delabVarInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcVar) := do
399-  match ← delab with
400-  | `($s:str) =>
401-      if isPlainName s.getString then
402-        `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
403-      else `(stlcVar| ~$s)
404-  | e => `(stlcVar| ~$e)
405-
406-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
407-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
408-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
409-  let stx ←
410-    match_expr ← getExpr with
411-    | Tm.tru => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
412-    | Tm.fls => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
413-    | Tm.var _ => do
414-        let x ← withAppArg delab
415-        match x with
416-        | `($s:str) =>
417-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
418-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
419-            else
420-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
421-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
422-        | _ =>
423-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
424-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
425-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
426-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
427-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
428-        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
429-    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
430-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
431-        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
432-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
433-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
434-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
435-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
436-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
437-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner

443-        if e.getAppFn.constName? == some `Stlc.subst && e.getAppNumArgs == 3 then
444-          let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
445-          let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
446-          let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
447-          `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
448-        else
449-          match ← delab with
450-          | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
451-          | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)

476---  END DETAILS
477-
478---  Here are the terms we will use as running examples, written in the new
479---  notation:
480-
481-abbrev idB := <{ λ x : Bool . x }>
482-
483-abbrev idBB := <{ λ x : Bool → Bool . x }>
484-
485-abbrev idBBBB := <{ λ x : (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) . x }>
486-
487-abbrev k := <{ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x }>
488-
489-abbrev notB := <{ λ x : Bool . if x then false else true }>
490-
491---  Note that an abstraction `λ x : T . t` (formally, `Tm.abs` applied to
492---  `x`, `T`, and `t`) is always annotated with the type `T` of its
493---  parameter, in contrast to Lean (and other functional languages like ML,
494---  Haskell, etc.), which use type inference to fill in missing
495---  annotations. We're not considering type inference at all here.
496-
497---  ## Operational Semantics
498-
499---  To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms, we begin, as always,
500---  by defining the set of values. Next, we define the critical notions of
501---  *free variables* and *substitution*, which are used in the reduction
502---  rule for application expressions. And finally we give the small-step
503---  relation itself.
504-
505---  ### Values
506-
507---  To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
508-
509---  First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear:
510---  `true` and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a
511---  value.
512-
513---  Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
514---  invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
515-
516---  Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
517-
518---  - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e.,
519---    only if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be
520---    without knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
521-
522---  - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t`
523---    is one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
524---    abstractions.
525-
526---  Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the first choice
527---  — for example,
528-
529-#reduce fun _x : Bool => 3 + 4
530-
531---  yields:
532-
533---    fun _x => 7
534-
535---  But Lean is rather unusual in this respect. Most functional programming
536---  languages make the second choice — reduction of a function's body only
537---  begins when the function is actually applied to an argument.
538-
539---  We also make the second choice here.
540-
541-inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
542-  | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
543-  | tru : Tm.IsValue <{ true }>
544-  | fls : Tm.IsValue <{ false }>
545-
546---  The example terms named above are all abstractions, hence all values.
547---  We record that once each, so that the reduction examples can cite the
548---  fact by name instead of unfolding the definition again at every use.
549-
550-theorem idB_value : idB.IsValue := .abs ..
551-theorem idBB_value : idBB.IsValue := .abs ..
552-theorem notB_value : notB.IsValue := .abs ..
553-
554---  Note to developers:
555---      The Rocq source follows each inductive definition in this chapter
556---      with a `Hint Constructors … : core`, registering the constructors
557---      with `auto`; the proofs then lean on `auto`/`eauto` to assemble
558---      derivations. We have no counterpart here: the proofs below name
559---      their constructors explicitly, in the style of the Types chapter.
560---      Lean's `grind` would be the closest analogue if a later pass wants
561---      automation.
562-
563---  ### STLC Programs
564-
565---  Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.
566-
567---  Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
568---  variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a
569---  STLC term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is,
570---  that contains no free variables.
571-
572---  (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often called an
573---  *open term*.)
574-
575---  Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
576---      Is the "shortly" above setting wrong expectations? Where exactly
577---      are we defining the free variables in a STLC term? BCP 25: Indeed,
578---      we need to define "free"!
579-
580---  Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions, we don't need
581---  to worry about whether variables are values, since we'll always be
582---  reducing programs "from the outside in," and that means the `step`
583---  relation will always be working with closed terms.
584-
585---  ### Substitution
586-
587---  Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of *substituting*
588---  one term for a variable in another term. This operation is used below
589---  to define the operational semantics of function application, where we
590---  will need to substitute the argument term for the function parameter in
591---  the function's body. For example, we reduce
592-
593---    (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
594-
595---  to
596-
597---    if false then true else false
598-
599---  by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the body of the
600---  function.
601-
602---  In general, we need to be able to substitute some given term `s` for
603---  occurrences of some variable `x` in another term `t`. Informally, this
604---  is written `[x:=s]t` and pronounced "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
605-
606---  Here are some examples:
607-
608---  - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
609---    `if true then true else false`
610-
611---  - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
612-
613---  - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields `if true then true else y`
614-
615---  - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
616-
617---  - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous substitution)
618-
619---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
620---    `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
621-
622---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
623-
624---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
625-
626---  - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
627-
628---  The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with `true` in
629---  `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`! The reason for this is
630---  that the `x` in the body of `λx:Bool. x` is *bound* by the abstraction:
631---  it is a new, local name that just happens to be spelled the same as
632---  some global name `x`.
633-
634---  Here is the definition, informally...
635-
636---    [x:=s]x               = s
637---    [x:=s]y               = y                     if x ≠ y
638---    [x:=s](λx:T. t)       = λx:T. t
639---    [x:=s](λy:T. t)       = λy:T. [x:=s]t         if x ≠ y
640---    [x:=s](t₁ t₂)         = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
641---    [x:=s]true            = true
642---    [x:=s]false           = false
643---    [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
644---                    if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
645-
646---  ... and formally:
647-
648-section
649-set_option hygiene false in
650-local macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
651-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
652-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
653-
654-def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
655-  match t with
656-  -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`
657-  -- (see the note below the definition).
658-  | .var y =>
659-      if x = y then s else t
660-  | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
661-      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
662-  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
663-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
664-  | <{ true }> =>
665-      <{ true }>
666-  | <{ false }> =>
667-      <{ false }>
668-  | <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
669-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
670-end
671-
672-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
673-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
674-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
675-
676---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: substitution)
677-
678---  One more line registers substitutions with the printer, so that a goal
679---  mentioning one reads as `[x := s] t` rather than as a `subst`
680---  application.
681-
682-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
683-@[delab app.Stlc.subst]
684-def delabSubst : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
685-  match ← delabTmInner with
686-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
687-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
688-
689---  END DETAILS
690-
691---  As we did for the evaluators in the Slang chapter, we pair the
692---  definition with one *simplification lemma* per constructor, saying how
693---  `subst` behaves on that constructor. The variable and abstraction cases
694---  each need two lemmas, since substitution treats a bound name
695---  differently depending on whether it is the name being substituted for.
696-
697-variable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty)
698-
699-@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
700-  simp [subst]
701-
702-@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
703-  simp [subst, h]
704-
705-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
706-  simp [subst]
707-
708-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
709-    <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
710-  simp [subst, h]
711-
712-@[simp] theorem subst_app :
713-    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
714-
715-@[simp] theorem subst_tru : <{ [~x := ~s] true }> = <{ true }> := rfl
716-
717-@[simp] theorem subst_fls : <{ [~x := ~s] false }> = <{ false }> := rfl
718-
719-@[simp] theorem subst_ite :
720-    <{ [~x := ~s] (if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
721-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl
722-
723---  _Quiz:_
724-
725---  What is the result of the following substitution?
726-
727---    [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
728-
729---  (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
730-
731---  (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
732-
733---  (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
734-
735---  (4) none of the above
736-
737---  *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if we
738---  consider the case where `s`, the term being substituted for a variable
739---  in some other term, may itself contain free variables. We say that `s`
740---  is an *open* term.
741-
742---  Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute the open
743---  term
744-
745---    s = λx:Bool. r
746-
747---  (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource) for the free
748---  variable `z` in the term
749-
750---    t = λr:Bool. z
751-
752---  where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
753-
754---    λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
755-
756---  where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured" by the
757---  binder at the beginning of `t`.
758-
759---  Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle that the names
760---  of bound variables do not matter. For example, if we rename the bound
761---  variable in `t`, e.g., let
762-
763---    t' = λw:Bool. z
764-
765---  then `[z:=s]t'` is
766-
767---    λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
768-
769---  which does not behave the same as the substituting in the original `t`:
770-
771---    [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
772-
773---  That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how `t` behaves
774---  under our simple substitution. So substitution gets more complicated in
775---  that setting, but fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
776---  variant.
777-
778---  Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining the `step`
779---  relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include
780---  binders for all of the variables they mention), we can sidestep this
781---  extra complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing richer
782---  languages.
783-
784---  ### Exercise (3 stars): substi_correct ⭐⭐⭐
785-
786---  The definition that we gave above defines substitution as a *function*.
787---  Suppose, instead, we wanted to define substitution as an inductive
788---  *relation* `Substi`. We've begun the definition by providing the
789---  `inductive` header and one of the constructors; your job is to fill in
790---  the rest of the constructors and prove that the relation you've defined
791---  coincides with the function given above.
792-
793-inductive Substi (s : Tm) (x : String) : Tm → Tm → Prop where
794-  | var1 :
795-      Substi s x (.var x) s
796-  | var2 (x' : String) (h : x ≠ x') :
797-      Substi s x (.var x') (.var x')
798-  | abs1 (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) :
799-      Substi s x <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }> <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
800-  | abs2 (x' : String) (T₁ : Ty) (t₁ t₁' : Tm)
801-      (hx : x ≠ x') (h : Substi s x t₁ t₁') :
802-      Substi s x <{ λ ~x' : ~T₁ . ~t₁ }> <{ λ ~x' : ~T₁ . ~t₁' }>
803-  | app (t₁ t₂ t₁' t₂' : Tm)
804-      (h₁ : Substi s x t₁ t₁') (h₂ : Substi s x t₂ t₂') :
805-      Substi s x <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> <{ ~t₁' ~t₂' }>
806-  | tru :
807-      Substi s x <{ true }> <{ true }>
808-  | fls :
809-      Substi s x <{ false }> <{ false }>
810-  | ite (t₁ t₂ t₃ t₁' t₂' t₃' : Tm)
811-      (h₁ : Substi s x t₁ t₁') (h₂ : Substi s x t₂ t₂') (h₃ : Substi s x t₃ t₃') :
812-      Substi s x <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂' else ~t₃' }>
813-
814-theorem substi_correct (s : Tm) (x : String) (t t' : Tm) :
815-    <{ [~x := ~s] ~t }> = t' ↔ Substi s x t t' := by
816-  constructor
817-  · -- →
818-    intro h
819-    subst h
820-    induction t with
821-    | var y =>
822-        by_cases hxy : x = y
823-        · subst hxy; simp; exact .var1
824-        · simp [hxy]; exact .var2 y hxy
825-    | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .app _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂
826-    | abs y T t₁ ih =>
827-        by_cases hxy : x = y
828-        · subst hxy; simp; exact .abs1 T t₁
829-        · simp [hxy]; exact .abs2 y T t₁ _ hxy ih
830-    | tru => exact .tru
831-    | fls => exact .fls
832-    | ite t₁ t₂ t₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃
833-  · -- ←
834-    intro h
835-    induction h <;> simp_all
836-
837---  ### Reduction
838-
839---  The small-step reduction relation for STLC now follows the same pattern
840---  as the ones we have seen before. Intuitively, to reduce a function
841---  application, we first reduce its left-hand side (the function) until it
842---  becomes an abstraction; then we reduce its right-hand side (the
843---  argument) until it is also a value; and finally we substitute the
844---  argument for the bound variable in the body of the abstraction. This
845---  last rule, written informally as
846-
847---    (λx:T. t₁₂) v₂ ⟶ [x:=v₂] t₁₂
848-
849---  is traditionally called *beta-reduction*.
850-
851---  v.IsValue
852---                         -----------------------      (appAbs)
853---                          (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
854-
855---                                t₁ ⟶ t₁'
856---                            ----------------          (app1)
857---                             t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
858-
859---                                v.IsValue
860---                                t₂ ⟶ t₂'
861---                            ----------------          (app2)
862---                             v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
863-
864---  ... plus the usual rules for conditionals:
865-
866---  --------------------------------                (ifTrue)
867---                     (if true then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₁
868-
869---                    ---------------------------------               (ifFalse)
870---                     (if false then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₂
871-
872---                                t₁ ⟶ t₁'
873---          ----------------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
874---           (if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) ⟶ (if t₁' then t₂ else t₃)
875-
876---  This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an application `(t₁ t₂)`,
877---  we
878-
879---  - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
880-
881---  - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
882-
883---  - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v` for the bound
884---    variable `x` in the body `t`.
885-
886---  Formally:
887-
888-section
889-set_option hygiene false in
890-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
891-
892-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
893-  | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
894-      <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
895-  | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
896-      <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
897-  | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
898-      <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
899-  | ifTrue (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :

1089---  ## Typing
1090-
1091---  Next we consider the typing relation of the STLC, which is meant to
1092---  prevent reduction from getting stuck.
1093-
1094---  For instance, the following two STLC terms are both stuck:
1095-
1096---  `if λx:Bool. x then true else false`
1097-
1098---  Here we branch on a function as though it were a boolean.
1099-
1100---  `true false`
1101-
1102---  Here we apply a boolean as though it were a function.
1103-
1104---  ### Contexts
1105-
1106---  Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
1107---  relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit
1108---  to make the definitions work.
1109-
1110---  Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively,
1111---  we need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed
1112---  the binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be
1113---  *open*). While checking that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`, we must remember
1114---  that `x` has type `T₁₁`, in order to deal with these free occurrences
1115---  of `x`. Similarly, `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and
1116---  typechecking their bodies could require looking up the declared types
1117---  of yet more free variables.
1118-
1119---  To keep track of all this, we add a third element to the relation, a
1120---  *typing context* `Γ`, which records the types of the variables that may
1121---  occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to
1122---  types.
1123-
1124---  The new *typing judgment* is written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and informally read as
1125---  "term `t` has type `T`, given the types of free variables in `t` as
1126---  specified by `Γ`".
1127-
1128---  We'll also write `x ↦ T ; Γ` for "update the partial map `Γ` so that it
1129---  maps `x` to `T`," following the notation from the `Typeclasses`
1130---  chapter.
1131-
1132---  With these refinements, we are ready to give informal and formal
1133---  specifications of the typing relation.
1134-
1135---  Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
1136---      I find the FULL explanation above much better than the TERSE one
1137---      below, since the question below seems ill-posed without extra
1138---      context. Why would one want to type a term `x y` if we've just said
1139---      that we will just look at closed terms as our programs?
1140-
1141-abbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
1142-
1143---  A context is a `PartialMap` from variable names to types — the partial
1144---  maps of the `Typeclasses` chapter, which are total maps whose values
1145---  are optional, so that `none` at a variable means "not bound here".
1146-
1147---  ### Typing Relation
1148-
1149---  Γ x = T₁
1150---                              ------------                       (var)
1151---                               Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T₁
1152-
1153---                          x ↦ T₂ ; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁
1154---                        -------------------------                (abs)
1155---                         Γ ⊢ λx:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1156-
1157---                            Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1158---                              Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂
1159---                           ------------------                    (app)
1160---                             Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ T₁
1161-
1162---                            -----------------                    (tru)
1163---                             Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
1164-
1165---                           ------------------                    (fls)
1166---                            Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
1167-
1168---               Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool    Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁    Γ ⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁
1169---              ---------------------------------------------      (ite)
1170---                     Γ ⊢ if t₁ then t₂ else t₃ ⦂ T₁
1171-
1172---  We can read the three-place relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` as: "under the
1173---  assumptions in Γ, the term `t` has the type `T`."
1174-
1175---  In the formal development, we write this judgment inside the same
1176---  `<{ .. }>` brackets we use for types and terms, as introduced by the
1177---  following notational conventions.
1178-
1179---  A context is written `∅` when empty and `x ↦ T ; Γ` when extended with
1180---  a binding, and `~e` escapes to a Lean expression of type `Context`. The
1181---  whole judgment then goes inside the same `<{ … }>` brackets as terms,
1182---  written with the turnstile and colon of the Types chapter:
1183---  `<{ Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`.
1184-
1185---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: contexts and judgments)
1186-
1187---  Contexts get a grammar of their own, `stlcCtx`. The **meaning** is the
1188---  map update we already have — `x ↦ T ; Γ` expands to exactly the
1189---  `Typeclasses` chapter's partial-map update on `Γ` — but its surface
1190---  syntax has to be our own, because inside these brackets all three
1191---  positions are in object syntax. Writing the map notation directly would
1192---  mean writing the binding as `"x" →ₚ <{ Bool → Bool }> ; Γ`: the name
1193---  quoted, and the type escaped back out of the brackets it belongs in.
1194---  The grammar hides those two encoding details, and nothing else.

1196-declare_syntax_cat stlcCtx
1197-syntax:max "∅" : stlcCtx
1198-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcCtx
1199-syntax:max stlcVar " ↦ " stlcTy " ; " stlcCtx : stlcCtx
1200-
1201-syntax:max (name := judgeBracket) "<{ " stlcCtx " ⊢ " stlcTm " ⦂ " stlcTy " }>" : term
1202-
1203-open Lean in
1204-/-- The `Context` denoted by a context expression. -/
1205-partial def ctxTerm (G : TSyntax `stlcCtx) : MacroM Term :=
1206-  match G with
1207-  | `(stlcCtx| ∅)   => `((∅ : Context))
1208-  | `(stlcCtx| ~$e) => pure e
1209-  | `(stlcCtx| $x:stlcVar ↦ $T:stlcTy ; $G:stlcCtx) => do
1210-      `(PartialMap.update $(← ctxTerm G) $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1211-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported

1213---  As with `subst`, the judgment notation is used inside the definition it
1214---  names, so it is introduced in two steps: the rule below is declared

1216---  the relation being declared, and after the `section` closes it is
1217---  declared again for real use.
1218-
1219-section
1220-set_option hygiene false in
1221-local macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1222-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1223-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)

1228-  | var (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ : Ty) (h : Γ[x] = some T₁) :
1229-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.var x) ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1230-  | abs (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm)
1231-      (h : <{ ~x ↦ ~T₂ ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1232-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>
1233-  | app (Γ : Context) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1234-      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₂ }>) :
1235-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1236-  | tru (Γ : Context) :
1237-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
1238-  | fls (Γ : Context) :
1239-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
1240-  | ite (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T₁ : Ty)

1242-      (h₃ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1243-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>

1264-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1265-/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1266-context prints as `x ↦ Bool ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1267-partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1268-  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1269-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T) => do
1270-      unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $T ; ∅))
1271-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1272-      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1273-      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1274-        if isPlainName x.getString then
1275-          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1276-        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1277-      match T with
1278-      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1279-      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1280-  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1281-
1282-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1283-@[app_unexpander Stlc.HasType]
1284-def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1285-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1286-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1287-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1288-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1289-  | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1290-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1291-  | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1292-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1293-  | _ => throw ()

1353-            ⦂ ~T }> :=

1355-    ⟨<{ (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) }>,
1356-     .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _

1360---  We can also show that some terms are *not* typable. For example, we can
1361---  check that there is no typing derivation assigning a type to the term
1362---  `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y` — i.e.,
1363-
1364---    ¬ ∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y ⦂ T

1366-example : ¬ ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x y ⦂ ~T }> := by
1367-  intro ⟨T, hc⟩
1368-  -- Each `cases` peels off one rule of the derivation, naming the premise it
1369-  -- leaves behind; the context stays small because the old hypothesis goes away.
1370-  cases hc with
1371-  | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1372-    cases h₁ with
1373-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₂ =>
1374-      cases h₂ with
1375-      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf _ =>
1376-        cases hf with
1377-        | var _ _ _ hx =>
1378-          -- `x` is bound to `Bool` in the context, but the application rule
1379-          -- needs it to have an arrow type.
1380-          exact Ty.noConfusion (Option.some.inj hx)

6-
7---  # Types: Type Systems
8-
9---  Note to developers:
10---      LATER: For consistency with the STLC definitions in future
11---      chapters, it would be better and simpler to represent numbers by a
12---      simple nat, rather than as strings of `succ` applied to `0` (which
13---      also introduces subtleties that are really not the main point
14---      here). But the present formulation is not a big problem either.
15---
16---      LATER: Harper's lecture from the Milner symposium would make a good
17---      support for this lecture.
18---
19---      LATER: There are a bunch of slides from earlier offerings of CIS500
20---      that might be wonderful additions to the TERSE notes.
21---      https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1002.pdf
22---      https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1004.pdf
23-
24---  Our next major topic is *type systems* — static program analyses that
25---  classify expressions according to the "shapes" of their results. We'll
26---  begin with a typed version of the simplest imaginable language, to
27---  introduce the basic ideas of types and typing rules and the fundamental
28---  theorems about type systems: *type preservation* and *progress*. In the
29---  next chapter we'll move on to the *simply typed lambda-calculus*, which
30---  lives at the core of every modern functional programming language
31---  (including Lean!).
32-
33---  ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
34-
35---  To motivate the discussion of type systems, let's begin as usual with a
36---  tiny toy language. We want it to have the potential for programs to go
37---  wrong because of runtime type errors, so we endow it with two kinds of
38---  data — numbers and booleans — where not every operation is defined on
39---  both types of data. For example, program terms like `5 + true` and
40---  `if 42 then 0 else 1` use undefined operator/data-type combinations.
41-
42---  The language definition is completely routine.
43-
44---  ### Syntax
45-
46---  Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
47-
48---  t ::= true
49---      | false
50---      | if t then t else t
51---      | 0
52---      | succ t
53---      | pred t
54---      | iszero t
55-
56---  And here it is formally:
57-
58-namespace TM
59-
60-inductive Tm where
61-  | tru
62-  | fls
63-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
64-  | zero
65-  | succ (t : Tm)
66-  | pred (t : Tm)
67-  | isZero (t : Tm)
68-
69---  #### Notation
70-
71---  Writing terms as raw constructors (`.ite .fls .zero (.succ .zero)`)
72---  gets unreadable quickly. We introduce a *concrete syntax* so that a
73---  term can be written inside `<{ … }>` — for example
74---  `<{ if false then 0 else succ 0 }>` — mirroring the informal grammar
75---  above. A bare identifier is spliced as a Lean term (so a variable `t`
76---  is written just `t`); `~e` escapes an arbitrary Lean expression, and
77---  `( … )` groups.
78-
79---  You do not need to understand exactly how the declarations below work;
80---  every object language in this book is given its syntax the same way, so
81---  it is worth seeing the pattern once:
82-
83---  - `declare_syntax_cat` adds a new non-terminal to Lean's grammar — here
84---    `tm`, the terms of this chapter's language.
85-
86---  - Each `syntax` directive declares one production of that non-terminal,
87---    with annotations fixing precedence, and the last one declares the
88---    `<{ … }>` brackets that let a `tm` appear where Lean expects a term.
89-
90---  - `macro_rules` then translates the resulting syntax forms into the
91---    corresponding constructors of `Tm`.
92-
93-declare_syntax_cat tm
94--- The keyword atoms (`true`/`false`/`succ`/`pred`/`iszero`) are parsed as bare
95--- identifiers and dispatched in the macro below, rather than declared as
96--- reserved symbols.  Reserving them would break ordinary Lean uses of
97--- `true`/`false` and clash with the constructor/case names `succ`, `pred`.
98-syntax:max num : tm
99-syntax:max ident : tm
100-syntax:75 ident ppHardSpace tm:76 : tm
101-syntax:max "(" tm ")" : tm
102-syntax:max "~" term:max : tm
103-syntax:50 "if " tm:51 " then " tm:51 " else " tm:51 : tm
104-syntax:max "<{ " tm " }>" : term
105-
106-open Lean in
107-macro_rules
108-  | `(<{ $n:num }>) =>
109-      if n.getNat == 0 then `(Tm.zero)
110-      else Macro.throwErrorAt n "the only numeric literal in this language is 0"
111-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
112-      match x.getId.toString with
113-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
114-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
115-      | _ => `($x)   -- a bare identifier is a spliced Lean term (usually a variable)
116-  | `(<{ $f:ident $e:tm }>) =>
117-      match f.getId.toString with
118-      | "succ"   => `(Tm.succ <{ $e }>)
119-      | "pred"   => `(Tm.pred <{ $e }>)
120-      | "iszero" => `(Tm.isZero <{ $e }>)
121-      | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt f s!"unknown operator `{f.getId}`"
122-  | `(<{ ($e) }>) => `(<{ $e }>)
123-  | `(<{ ~$e }>)  => pure e
124-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) => `(Tm.ite <{ $c }> <{ $t }> <{ $e }>)
125-
126---  A *delaborator* closes the loop: it walks a `Tm` value and rebuilds the
127---  concrete syntax, so that terms appearing in goals, `#check`, and
128---  `#eval` output print as `<{ … }>` rather than as a pile of
129---  constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns it off, revealing the
130---  raw constructors.) A `Ty` prints as `Bool` or `Nat`.
131-
132---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing terms back)
133-
134-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
135-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `tm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
136-@[category_parenthesizer tm]
137-def tm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
138-  maybeParenthesize `tm true wrapParens prec <|
139-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `tm prec
140-where
141-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
142-    let pstx ← `(tm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
143-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
144-
145-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
146-/-- Rebuild `tm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` term. -/
147-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `tm) := do
148-  let stx ←
149-    match_expr ← getExpr with
150-    | Tm.tru => `(tm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
151-    | Tm.fls => `(tm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
152-    | Tm.zero => `(tm| 0)
153-    | Tm.succ _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
154-    | Tm.pred _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
155-    | Tm.isZero _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `iszero):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
156-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
157-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
158-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
159-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
160-        `(tm| if $c then $t else $e)
161-    | _ => do
162-        -- A bare variable prints without the `~` escape; anything else keeps it.
163-        match ← delab with
164-        | `($i:ident) => `(tm| $i:ident)
165-        | e => `(tm| ~$e)
166-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
167-
168-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
169--- The keys are the constants' full names: `Tm` lives in namespace `TM`, and the
170--- `delab` attribute does not resolve its argument against the current namespace.
171-@[delab app.TM.Tm.tru, delab app.TM.Tm.fls, delab app.TM.Tm.zero, delab app.TM.Tm.succ,
172-  delab app.TM.Tm.pred, delab app.TM.Tm.isZero, delab app.TM.Tm.ite]
173-partial def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
174-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
175-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.zero => true
176-    | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true | Tm.isZero _ => true
177-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true | _ => false
178-  match ← delabTmInner with
179-  | `(tm| ~$e) => pure e
180-  | e => `(<{ $e }>)
181-
182---  END DETAILS
183-
184---  #### Values
185-
186---  *Values* are `true`, `false`, and numeric values (`0`, and `succ` of a
187---  numeric value).
188-
189-inductive Tm.IsBValue : Tm → Prop where
190-  | tru : Tm.IsBValue <{ true }>
191-  | fls : Tm.IsBValue <{ false }>
192-
193-inductive Tm.IsNValue : Tm → Prop where
194-  | zero : Tm.IsNValue <{ 0 }>
195-  | succ (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNValue <{ succ t }>
196-
197-def Tm.IsValue (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsBValue t ∨ Tm.IsNValue t
198-
199---  ### Operational Semantics
200-
201---  Here is the single-step relation, informally.
202-
203---  -----------------------------                 (ifTrue)
204---                     if true then t1 else t2 ⟶ t1
205-
206---                     ------------------------------                (ifFalse)
207---                     if false then t1 else t2 ⟶ t2
208-
209---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
210---              -----------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
211---              if t1 then t2 else t3 ⟶ if t1' then t2 else t3
212-
213---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
214---                           -------------------                     (succStep)
215---                           succ t1 ⟶ succ t1'
216-
217---                             -----------                           (predZero)
218---                             pred 0 ⟶ 0
219-
220---                              IsNValue v
221---                          ------------------                       (predSucc)
222---                          pred (succ v) ⟶ v
223-
224---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
225---                           -------------------                     (predStep)
226---                           pred t1 ⟶ pred t1'
227-
228---                            ----------------                       (isZeroZero)
229---                            iszero 0 ⟶ true
230-
231---                               IsNValue v
232---                        ------------------------                   (isZeroSucc)
233---                        iszero (succ v) ⟶ false
234-
235---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
236---                         -----------------------                   (isZeroStep)
237---                         iszero t1 ⟶ iszero t1'
238-
239---  The formal rules are below. We are defining them differently than we
240---  have previously: We are using the relation's own notation (`⟶`) inside
241---  the constructors. We achieve this by defining `Tm.Step` within a
242---  `section`, and within that section using `set_option hygiene false` on
243---  `⟶` so that the constructors read in this syntax; after the `section`
244---  closes, we use a `scoped notation` as we have done before.
245-
246-section
247-set_option hygiene false in
248-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
249-inductive Tm.Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
250-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t1
251-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t2
252-  | ifStep (c c' t2 t3 : Tm) (h : c ⟶ c') :
253-      <{ if c then t2 else t3 }> ⟶ <{ if c' then t2 else t3 }>
254-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ succ t1 }> ⟶ <{ succ t1' }>
255-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⟶ <{ 0 }>
256-  | predSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ pred (succ v) }> ⟶ v
257-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ pred t1 }> ⟶ <{ pred t1' }>
258-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⟶ <{ true }>
259-  | isZeroSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ iszero (succ v) }> ⟶ <{ false }>
260-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ iszero t1 }> ⟶ <{ iszero t1' }>
261-end
262-
263-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
264-
265---  The `Tm.IsNValue` premises in `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc` are needed
266---  for determinism (this will be proved in an optional exercise below).
267-
268---  Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about whether the
269---  expression being stepped makes global sense — it just checks that the
270---  operation in the *next* reduction step is being applied to the right
271---  kinds of operands. For example, the term `succ true` cannot take a
272---  step, but the almost as obviously nonsensical term
273-
274---  succ (if true then true else true)
275-
276---  can take a step (once, before becoming stuck).
277-
278---  ### Normal Forms and Values
279-
280---  The first interesting thing to notice about this `Tm.Step` relation is
281---  that the strong progress theorem from the Smallstep chapter fails here.
282---  That is, there are terms that are normal forms (they can't take a step)
283---  but not values (they are not included in our definition of possible
284---  "results of reduction").
285-
286---  Such terms are *stuck*.
287-
288-def Tm.IsNormalForm (t : Tm) : Prop := _root_.IsNormalForm Tm.Step t
289-
290-def Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsNormalForm t ∧ ¬ Tm.IsValue t
291-
292---  ### Exercise (2 stars): some_term_is_stuck ⭐⭐
293-
294-theorem some_term_is_stuck : ∃ t, Tm.IsStuck t := by
295-  refine ⟨<{ succ false }>, ?_, ?_⟩
296-  · intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
297-    cases hstp with
298-    | succStep _ _ h => cases h
299-  · intro h
300-    cases h with
301-    | inl hb => cases hb
302-    | inr hn => cases hn with | succ _ h => cases h
303-
304---  However, although values and normal forms are *not* the same in this
305---  language, the set of values is a subset of the set of normal forms.
306-
307---  This is important because it shows we did not accidentally define
308---  things so that some value could still take a step.
309-
310-theorem nvalue_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
311-  induction h with
312-  | zero => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
313-  | succ t0 hn0 ih =>
314-      intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
315-      cases hstp with
316-      | succStep _ t1' h => exact ih ⟨t1', h⟩
317-
318---  ### Exercise (3 stars): value_is_nf ⭐⭐⭐
319-
320---  (Hint: You will reach a point in this proof where you need to use an
321---  induction to reason about a term that is known to be a numeric value.
322---  This induction can be performed either over the term itself or over the
323---  evidence that it is a numeric value. The proof goes through in either
324---  case, but you will find that one way is quite a bit shorter than the
325---  other. For the sake of the exercise, try to complete the proof both
326---  ways.)
327-
328-theorem value_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
329-  cases h with
330-  | inl hb => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hb <;> cases hstp
331-  | inr hn => exact nvalue_is_nf t hn
332-
333---  The "other way" mentioned in the hint proves the same fact by induction
334---  on the term itself rather than on the evidence that it is a numeric
335---  value. It goes through, but is a bit longer than the `nvalue_is_nf`
336---  route above.
337-
338-theorem value_is_nf' : ∀ t, Tm.IsValue t → Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
339-  intro t
340-  induction t with
341-  | tru => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
342-  | fls => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
343-  | ite c t0 e _ _ _ =>
344-      intro h; cases h with
345-      | inl hb => cases hb
346-      | inr hn => cases hn
347-  | zero => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
348-  | succ t0 ih =>
349-      -- The `succ` case is the only one that doesn't immediately present a
350-      -- contradiction.  Considering how a `succ` term can be a value, it is
351-      -- syntactically not a boolean value, but the numeric value case
352-      -- requires a bit more work.
353-      intro h hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
354-      cases hstp with
355-      | succStep _ t1' hstp' =>
356-          cases h with
357-          | inl hb => cases hb
358-          -- By the IH, if `t0` is a numeric value, then it can not step.
359-          | inr hn => cases hn with
360-            | succ _ hn0 => exact ih (.inr hn0) ⟨t1', hstp'⟩
361-  | pred t0 _ =>
362-      intro h; cases h with
363-      | inl hb => cases hb
364-      | inr hn => cases hn
365-  | isZero t0 _ =>
366-      intro h; cases h with
367-      | inl hb => cases hb
368-      | inr hn => cases hn
369-
370---  ### Exercise (3 stars): step_deterministic (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
371-
372---  Use `value_is_nf` (here, `nvalue_is_nf`) to show that the `Tm.Step`
373---  relation is also deterministic.
374-
375-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Tm.Step := by
376-  intro x y1 y2 h1
377-  induction h1 generalizing y2 with
378-  | ifTrue t1 t2 =>
379-      intro h2; cases h2 with
380-      | ifTrue => rfl
381-      | ifStep _ _ _ _ hc => cases hc
382-  | ifFalse t1 t2 =>
383-      intro h2; cases h2 with
384-      | ifFalse => rfl
385-      | ifStep _ _ _ _ hc => cases hc
386-  | ifStep c c' t2 t3 hc ih =>
387-      intro h2; cases h2 with
388-      | ifTrue => cases hc
389-      | ifFalse => cases hc
390-      | ifStep _ c'' _ _ hc2 => rw [ih _ hc2]
391-  | succStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
392-      intro h2; cases h2 with
393-      | succStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
394-  | predZero =>
395-      intro h2; cases h2 with
396-      | predZero => rfl
397-      | predStep _ _ hs => cases hs
398-  | predSucc v hv =>
399-      intro h2; cases h2 with
400-      | predSucc => rfl
401-      | predStep _ _ hs => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ v hv))
402-  | predStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
403-      intro h2; cases h2 with
404-      | predZero => cases hs
405-      | predSucc _ hv => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ _ hv))
406-      | predStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
407-  | isZeroZero =>
408-      intro h2; cases h2 with
409-      | isZeroZero => rfl
410-      | isZeroStep _ _ hs => cases hs
411-  | isZeroSucc v hv =>
412-      intro h2; cases h2 with
413-      | isZeroSucc => rfl
414-      | isZeroStep _ _ hs => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ v hv))
415-  | isZeroStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
416-      intro h2; cases h2 with
417-      | isZeroZero => cases hs
418-      | isZeroSucc _ hv => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ _ hv))
419-      | isZeroStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
420-

453---  (Hint: Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about whether
454---  the expression being stepped makes global sense — it just checks that
455---  the operation in the *next* reduction step is being applied to the

458---  *Optional aside, good practice with step relations but tangential to
459---  the main development.* We define an alternate step relation `⇢` and a
460---  step *function* for it.
461-
462---  Note to developers (mwhicks1):
463---      `In the Rocq source these were a hidden, never-uncommented draft

467---  Suppose we define an alternate single-step relation, written `t ⇢ t'`,
468---  that *drops* the `Tm.IsNValue` premise from the `predSucc` and
469---  `isZeroSucc` rules — so `pred (succ t)` and `iszero (succ t)` may step
470---  even when `t` is not a numeric value. (It is built with exactly the
471---  same notation setup as `Tm.Step`; note `predSucc`/`isZeroSucc` no
472---  longer take a premise.)
473-
474-section
475-set_option hygiene false in
476-local notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
477-inductive Tm.AltStep : Tm → Tm → Prop where
478-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t1
479-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t2
480-  | ifStep (t1 t1' t2 t3 : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' →
481-      <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> ⇢ <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
482-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ succ t1 }> ⇢ <{ succ t1' }>
483-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⇢ <{ 0 }>
484-  | predSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ pred (succ t1) }> ⇢ t1
485-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ pred t1 }> ⇢ <{ pred t1' }>
486-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⇢ <{ true }>
487-  | isZeroSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ iszero (succ t1) }> ⇢ <{ false }>
488-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ iszero t1 }> ⇢ <{ iszero t1' }>
489-end

491-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'

493---  Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
494-
495---  - Is `⇢` deterministic (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
496---    `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by `predSucc`) and
497---    `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
498-
499---  - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form? No:
500---    `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but steps under `⇢` (to
501---    `true`, by `predSucc`, now that the `Tm.IsNValue` premise is gone).
502-
503---  - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form? Yes —
504---    `Tm.Step` is a subrelation of `⇢`, so anything stuck for `⇢` is stuck
505---    for `Tm.Step`.
506-
507---  - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps) also reachable
508---    by `⇢` (in many steps)? Yes, for the same subrelation reason.
509-
510---  - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value `false` under
511---    `⇢` but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
512-
513---  A *functional* version computes a single `⇢` step of a term, returning
514---  `none` when the term is a `⇢` normal form. This is a nice chance to see
515---  a step *function*, which the chapter otherwise gives only as a
516---  relation:
517-
518-def alt_simplify_step (t : Tm) : Option Tm :=
519-  match t with
520-  | <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> =>
521-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
522-      | some t1' => some <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
523-      | none =>
524-        match t1 with
525-        | <{ true }>  => some t2
526-        | <{ false }> => some t3
527-        | _           => none
528-  | <{ succ t1 }> =>
529-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
530-      | some t1' => some <{ succ t1' }>
531-      | none     => none
532-  | <{ pred t1 }> =>
533-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
534-      | some t1' => some <{ pred t1' }>
535-      | none =>
536-        match t1 with
537-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ 0 }>
538-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some t2
539-        | _             => none
540-  | <{ iszero t1 }> =>
541-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
542-      | some t1' => some <{ iszero t1' }>
543-      | none =>
544-        match t1 with
545-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ true }>
546-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some <{ false }>
547-        | _             => none
548-  | _ => none
549-
550--- `pred (succ true)` steps under `⇢` (the dropped `IsNValue` premise) even
551--- though it is stuck under `Tm.Step`:
552-example : alt_simplify_step <{ pred (succ true) }> = some <{ true }> := rfl
553-example : alt_simplify_step <{ if true then 0 else succ 0 }> = some <{ 0 }> := rfl
554-example : alt_simplify_step <{ 0 }> = none := rfl

556---  ### Typing
557-
558---  The next critical observation is that, although this language has stuck
559---  terms, they are always nonsensical, mixing booleans and numbers in a
560---  way that we don't even *want* to have a meaning. We can easily exclude
561---  such ill-typed terms by defining a *typing relation* that relates terms
562---  to the types (either numeric or boolean) of their final results.
563-
564---  The *typing relation* `⊢ t ⦂ T` relates terms to the types of their
565---  results. In informal notation it is often written `⊢ t ⦂ T` and
566---  pronounced "`t` has type `T`." The `⊢` symbol is called a "turnstile."
567---  The `⦂` between the term and its type is a dedicated type-colon glyph
568---  (distinct from an ordinary `:`); in the editor you enter it with the
569---  Lean input abbreviation `\tc` followed by a space. Below, we're going
570---  to see richer typing relations where one or more additional "context"
571---  arguments are written to the left of the turnstile. For the moment, the
572---  context is always empty.
573-
574---  -------------                (tru)
575---                       ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
576-
577---                       --------------               (fls)
578---                       ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
579-
580---            ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool    ⊢ t2 ⦂ T    ⊢ t3 ⦂ T
581---            -----------------------------------     (ite)
582---                ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T
583-
584---                         ---------                  (zero)
585---                         ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat
586-
587---                        ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
588---                      ---------------               (succ)
589---                      ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat
590-
591---                        ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
592---                      ---------------               (pred)
593---                      ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat
594-
595---                        ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
596---                     ------------------             (isZero)
597---                     ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool
598-
599---  Here are the formal rules.
600-
601---  The typing judgment is written `<{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`: the whole judgment is
602---  wrapped in `<{ … }>`, the term is in the object grammar (bare
603---  variables, no inner `<{ }>`) and the type as `Bool`/`Nat` (a type
604---  variable is spliced, `~T` escapes to a Lean `Ty`). As with `Tm.Step`,
605---  we define the relation using its own notation, inside a `section` with
606---  `set_option hygiene false` so the bare name `Tm.HasType` in the
607---  expansion resolves to the relation being defined; after the `section`
608---  we re-declare the same rules hygienically for real use. Unlike `⟶`, the
609---  judgment builds on the custom `tm` syntactic category, so it must use
610---  `syntax`/`macro_rules` rather than `notation` — which is why it still
611---  needs the `app_unexpander` to print the judgment back.
612-
613-inductive Ty where
614-  | bool
615-  | nat
616-
617-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " ident " }>" : term
618-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " "~" term:max " }>" : term
619-
620-section
621-set_option hygiene false in
622-local macro_rules
623-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
624-      match T.getId.toString with
625-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
626-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
627-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
628-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
629-
630--- The actual definition, written in the notation above.
631-inductive Tm.HasType : Tm → Ty → Prop where
632-  | tru : <{ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
633-  | fls : <{ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
634-  | ite (t1 t2 t3 : Tm) (T : Ty)
635-      (h1 : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool }>) (h2 : <{ ⊢ t2 ⦂ T }>) (h3 : <{ ⊢ t3 ⦂ T }>) :
636-      <{ ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T }>
637-  | zero : <{ ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat }>
638-  | succ (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat }>
639-  | pred (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat }>
640-  | isZero (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool }>
641-end
642-
643--- The same rules repeated with hygiene enabled, for use after the section.
644-macro_rules
645-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
646-      match T.getId.toString with
647-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
648-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
649-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
650-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
651-
652--- Print `Tm.HasType`/`Ty` values back as `<{ ⊢ … ⦂ … }>` notation: `delabTy`
653-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
654-@[delab app.TM.Ty.bool, delab app.TM.Ty.nat]
655-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
656-  match_expr ← getExpr with
657-  | Ty.bool => `($(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
658-  | Ty.nat  => `($(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
659-  | _ => failure
660-
661-@[app_unexpander Tm.HasType]
662-def Tm.HasType.unexpand : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
663-  | `($_ <{ $t }> $T:ident) => `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
664-  | `($_ $t:ident $T:ident)  => `(<{ ⊢ $(⟨t.raw⟩) ⦂ $T }>)
665-  | `($_ $t $T)              => `(<{ ⊢ ~$t ⦂ ~$T }>)
666-  | _ => throw ()
667-
668-example : <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else succ 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
669-  .ite _ _ _ _ .fls .zero (.succ _ .zero)
670-
671---  It's important to realize that the typing relation is a *conservative*
672---  (or *static*) approximation: it does not consider what happens when the
673---  term is reduced — in particular, it does not calculate the type of its
674---  normal form.
675-
676-example : ¬ <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
677-  intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
678-
679-example :
680-    ¬ <{ ⊢ if iszero (succ 0) then succ false else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
681-  intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
