688---  ### Canonical forms
689-
690---  The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact that the
691---  definitions of boolean and numeric values agree with the typing
692---  relation: a well-typed value of type `Bool` is a boolean value, and of
693---  type `Nat` a numeric value.
694-
695-theorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
696-  cases hv with
697-  | inl hb => exact hb
698-  | inr hn => cases hn with
699-    | zero => cases hT
700-    | succ t0 h => cases hT
701-
702-theorem nat_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNValue t := by
703-  cases hv with
704-  | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
705-  | inr hn => exact hn
706-
707---  ### Progress
708-
709---  The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
710-
711---  The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or
712---  conversely, if a term is well typed, then either it is a value or it
713---  can take at least one step. We call this *progress*.
714-
715---  ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress ⭐⭐⭐
716-
717---  Complete the formal proof of the `progress` property. (Make sure you
718---  understand the parts we've given of the informal proof in the following
719---  exercise before starting — this will save you a lot of time.)
720-
721-theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) : Tm.IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
722-  induction hT with
723-  | tru => exact .inl (.inl .tru)
724-  | fls => exact .inl (.inl .fls)
725-  | zero => exact .inl (.inr .zero)
726-  | ite t1 t2 t3 T h1 h2 h3 ih1 ih2 ih3 =>
727-      right
728-      cases ih1 with
729-      | inl hv1 =>
730-          cases bool_canonical t1 h1 hv1 with
731-          | tru => exact ⟨t2, .ifTrue t2 t3⟩
732-          | fls => exact ⟨t3, .ifFalse t2 t3⟩
733-      | inr hs1 => obtain ⟨t1', h⟩ := hs1
734-                   exact ⟨<{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>, .ifStep t1 t1' t2 t3 h⟩
735-  | succ t1 h ih =>
736-      cases ih with
737-      | inl hv => exact .inl (.inr (.succ t1 (nat_canonical t1 h hv)))
738-      | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact .inr ⟨<{ succ t' }>, .succStep t1 t' h'⟩
739-  | pred t1 h ih =>
740-      right
741-      cases ih with
742-      | inl hv =>
743-          cases nat_canonical t1 h hv with
744-          | zero => exact ⟨<{ 0 }>, .predZero⟩
745-          | succ t0 hn0 => exact ⟨t0, .predSucc t0 hn0⟩
746-      | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ pred t' }>, .predStep t1 t' h'⟩
747-  | isZero t1 h ih =>
748-      right
749-      cases ih with
750-      | inl hv =>
751-          cases nat_canonical t1 h hv with
752-          | zero => exact ⟨<{ true }>, .isZeroZero⟩
753-          | succ t0 hn0 => exact ⟨<{ false }>, .isZeroSucc t0 hn0⟩
754-      | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ iszero t' }>, .isZeroStep t1 t' h'⟩
755-

762-
763---  (B) Progress implies strong progress
764-

776---      Check the typesetting of this...
777-
778---  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else `t ⟶ t'`
779---  for some `t'`.
780-
781---  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
782-
783---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
784---    `t = if t1 then t2
785---        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
786---    `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
787---    to some `t1'`.
788-
789---    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact
790---      that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value
791---      (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e., it is either `true` or `false`. If
792---      `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by `ifTrue`, while if
793---      `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`. Either way, `t`
794---      can step, which is what we wanted to show.
795-
796---    - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`, so can `t`.
797-
798---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `tru`, then `t = true`, which
799---    is a boolean value and hence a value.  The cases for `fls` and `zero`
800---    are similar.
801-
802---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `succ`, then `t = succ t1`, with
803---    `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
804---    to some `t1'`.
805-
806---    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemma `t1` is an
807---      `nvalue`, and hence `t` is also an `nvalue` (and hence a value) by
808---      `succ`.
809-
810---    - If `t1` can take a step, then by `succStep`, so can `t`.
811-
812---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `pred`, then `t = pred t1`, with
813---    `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
814---    to some `t1'`.
815-
816---    - If `t1` is a value, then (by the same argument as in the previous
817---      case) it must be an `nvalue`.  By case analysis on the `nvalue`
818---      judgement, there are two cases:
819-
820---      - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `predZero`.
821-
822---      - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'`, with `t1'` an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
823---        again take a step, this time by `predSucc`.
824-
825---    - Finally, if `t1` can take a step, then by `predStep`, so can `t`.
826-
827---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `isZero`, then `t = iszero t1`,
828---    with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` steps
829---    to some `t1'`.
830-
831---    - If `t1` is a value, it must be an `nvalue`, and there are two cases to
832---      consider:
833-
834---      - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `isZeroZero`.
835-
836---      - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'` where `t1'` is an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
837---        take a step by `isZeroSucc`.
838-
839---    - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `isZeroStep`.
840-
841---  This theorem is more interesting than the strong progress theorem that
842---  we saw in the Smallstep chapter, where *all* normal forms were values.
843---  Here a term can be stuck, but only if it is ill typed.

878---  ### Type Preservation
879-
880---  The second critical property of typing is that, when a well-typed term
881---  takes a step, the result is a well-typed term (of the same type).
882-
883---  ### Exercise (2 stars): finish_preservation ⭐⭐
884-
885---  Complete the formal proof of the `preservation` property. (Again, make
886---  sure you understand the informal proof fragment in the following
887---  exercise first.)
888-
889-theorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (he : t ⟶ t') : <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> := by
890-  induction hT generalizing t' with
891-  | tru => cases he
892-  | fls => cases he
893-  | zero => cases he
894-  | ite t1 t2 t3 T h1 h2 h3 ih1 ih2 ih3 =>
895-      cases he with
896-      | ifTrue => exact h2
897-      | ifFalse => exact h3
898-      | ifStep _ c' _ _ hc => exact .ite c' t2 t3 T (ih1 c' hc) h2 h3
899-  | succ t1 h ih =>
900-      cases he with
901-      | succStep _ t1' hs => exact .succ t1' (ih t1' hs)
902-  | pred t1 h ih =>
903-      cases he with
904-      | predZero => exact .zero
905-      | predSucc v hv => cases h with | succ _ hh => exact hh
906-      | predStep _ t1' hs => exact .pred t1' (ih t1' hs)
907-  | isZero t1 h ih =>
908-      cases he with
909-      | isZeroZero => exact .tru
910-      | isZeroSucc v hv => exact .fls
911-      | isZeroStep _ t1' hs => exact .isZero t1' (ih t1' hs)

913---  ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_preservation_informal (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
914-
915---  Complete the following informal proof.
916-
917---  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T` and `t ⟶ t'`, then `⊢ t' ⦂ T`.
918-
919---  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
920-
921---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
922---    `t = if t1 then t2
923---        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
924---    `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`.
925-
926---    Inspecting the rules for the small-step reduction relation and
927---    remembering that `t` has the form `if ...`, we see that the only ones
928---    that could have been used to prove `t ⟶ t'` are `ifTrue`, `ifFalse`,
929---    or `ifStep`.
930-
931---    - If the last rule was `ifTrue`, then `t' = t2`. But we know that
932---      `⊢ t2 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
933-
934---    - If the last rule was `ifFalse`, then `t' = t3`. But we know that
935---      `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`, so we are done.

991-theorem preservation' (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (he : t ⟶ t') : <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> := by
992-  induction he generalizing T with
993-  | ifTrue t1 t2 => cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => exact h2
994-  | ifFalse t1 t2 => cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => exact h3
995-  | ifStep c c' t2 t3 hc ih =>
996-      cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => exact .ite c' t2 t3 T (ih .bool h1) h2 h3
997-  | succStep t1 t1' hs ih => cases hT with | succ _ h => exact .succ t1' (ih .nat h)
998-  | predZero => cases hT with | pred _ h => exact .zero
999-  | predSucc v hv => cases hT with | pred _ h => cases h with | succ _ hh => exact hh
1000-  | predStep t1 t1' hs ih => cases hT with | pred _ h => exact .pred t1' (ih .nat h)
1001-  | isZeroZero => cases hT with | isZero _ h => exact .tru
1002-  | isZeroSucc v hv => cases hT with | isZero _ h => exact .fls
1003-  | isZeroStep t1 t1' hs ih => cases hT with | isZero _ h => exact .isZero t1' (ih .nat h)

1005---  The preservation theorem is often called *subject reduction*, because
1006---  it tells us what happens when the "subject" of the typing relation is
1007---  reduced. This terminology comes from thinking of typing statements as
1008---  sentences, where the term is the subject and the type is the predicate.

1012---  Putting progress and preservation together, we see that a well-typed
1013---  term can never reach a stuck state.

1015-def Tm.MultiStep (t1 t2 : Tm) : Prop := Multi Tm.Step t1 t2

1019-theorem soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ Tm.IsStuck t' := by
1020-  induction hm generalizing T with
1021-  | refl a =>
1022-      intro hst; obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
1023-      cases progress a T hT with
1024-      | inl hv => exact hnv hv
1025-      | inr hs => exact hnf hs
1026-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact ih T (preservation a b T hT h1)

1057---  ### Exercise (3 stars): subject_expansion ⭐⭐⭐
1058-
1059---  Having seen the subject reduction property, one might wonder whether
1060---  the opposite property — subject *expansion* — also holds. That is, is
1061---  it always the case that, if `t ⟶ t'` and `⊢ t' ⦂ T`, then `⊢ t ⦂ T`? If
1062---  so, prove it. If not, give a counter-example.
1063-
1064---  Subject expansion does not hold in this language (or most interesting
1065---  languages).  For example, `if false then true else 0` is ill typed, but
1066---  it reduces to the well-typed term `0`.
1067-
1068-theorem subject_expansion :
1069-    (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>)
1070-    ∨ ¬ (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) := by
1071-  right
1072-  intro hse
1073-  have hT : <{ ⊢ if false then true else 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
1074-    hse <{ if false then true else 0 }> <{ 0 }> .nat ⟨.ifFalse <{ true }> <{ 0 }>, .zero⟩
1075-  cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
1076-

1184---  ### Exercise (1 star): remove_pred0 (manually graded) ⭐
1185-
1186---  The reduction rule `predZero` is a bit counter-intuitive: we might feel
1187---  that it makes more sense for the predecessor of `0` to be undefined,
1188---  rather than being defined to be `0`. Can we achieve this simply by
1189---  removing the rule from the definition of `Tm.Step`? Would doing so
1190---  create any problems elsewhere?
1191-
1192---  Yes, but doing this would break the progress property.  A better way would
1193---  be to raise an exception in this case, but this requires that we add
1194---  exceptions to the language we're formalizing!

1196---  ### Exercise (4 stars): prog_pres_bigstep (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1197-
1198---  Suppose our evaluation relation is defined in the big-step style. State
1199---  appropriate analogs of the progress and preservation properties. (You
1200---  do not need to prove them.)
1201-
1202---  Can you see any limitations of either of your properties? Do they allow
1203---  for nonterminating programs? Why might we prefer the small-step
1204---  semantics for stating preservation and progress?
1205-
1206---  The type preservation property for the big-step semantics is similar to
1207---  the one we gave for the small-step semantics: if a well-typed term
1208---  evaluates to some final value, then this value has the same type as the
1209---  original term.  The proof is similar to the one we gave.  However,
1210---  preservation for small-step semantics implies that all intermediate states
1211---  (i.e., all states reachable in multi-step) are well-typed, whereas big-step
1212---  semantics only relates a term to its final evaluation result, with no
1213---  notion of "intermediate state" about which preservation can make
1214---  guarantees.
1215-
1216---  The situation with the progress property is more interesting.  A direct
1217---  analog (if a term is well typed then it evaluates to some other term)
1218---  makes a much stronger claim than the progress theorem we have given: it
1219---  says that every well-typed term can be evaluated to some final value---that
1220---  is, that evaluation always terminates on well-typed terms.  For arithmetic
1221---  expressions, this happens to be the case, but for more interesting
1222---  languages (languages involving general recursion, for example) it will
1223---  often not be true.  For such languages, we simply have no progress property
1224---  in the big-step style: in effect, there is no way to tell the difference
1225---  between reaching an error state and failing to terminate.  This is one
1226---  reason that language theorists generally prefer the small-step style.
